activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
story:
The keys were cold in Mason's hand when he slid them into the ignition, and Mr. Sánchez, who had taught half the neighbourhood's kids to drive out of the same cracked driveway, settled into the passenger seat and said, "Mirror, signal, shoulder check. Then and only then, reverse."

Mason had turned eighteen two weeks ago and passed the written test the same afternoon, and all week he had been composing the message he would send once the lesson was over: I can drive. He had not sent it yet, because it wasn't technically true, but it felt true the way a thing feels true when it is only hours away. Elyse and Syed were coming at noon. The plan was his plan, laid out over fries on Friday: he would get his license this month, and on the last Saturday of June they would drive to the lake, all three of them, windows down, no parent in the car, no one asking when they'd be home.

"Feet off both pedals," Mr. Sánchez said. "Let the car roll on idle. It knows more than you do right now."

The car crept backward down the driveway, and Mason held the wheel too tight, and the mailbox loomed in the mirror like a judge. He straightened, braked, and sat there breathing. Last summer his mother had stood in this exact spot, arms crossed, watching him back his grandfather's truck into the fence post. The crack in the post was still there, a grey seam in the wood. He had not driven anything since. She had made him hand over the keys before he could argue, and the argument he had swallowed had sat in him for a year, heavy and undelivered, like a remittance he kept meaning to send and never did.

"Again," said Mr. Sánchez. "This time you steer before you need to, not after."

At eleven forty, wheels crunched at the curb. Elyse climbed out of Syed's brother's car with a duffel bag and a folded blanket, and Syed followed with a cooler, and they both stood on the lawn looking at Mason's putative chariot, a faded sedan with a learner's sign suctioned to the rear window. Mason eased the car forward to the top of the driveway and cut the engine.

"So you're basically done, right?" Elyse said. "One lesson and you're a driver."

"One lesson and I'm a learner," Mason said. "That's the whole word on the permit. Learner."

Syed squinted at him. "So what, you drive for a year and then you're free?"

"It's not a year." Mason had read the handbook twice on the bus, cover to cover, and the shape of it had already knocked the shine off Saturday. "It's the permit first. Then there's a road test, and if you pass you don't get a full license. You get a provisional one. It has restrictions on it. Then, after that, the full license."

"Restrictions like what?" Elyse asked, and her voice had gone flat in the way it did when she was deciding whether to be angry.

"I'm reading the details tonight," Mason said, which was mostly true, and he knew enough already to know the honest answer to the question she was actually asking. "I can't drive you guys around right away. Not as a brand-new driver. It's graduated licensing. It goes permit, then provisional, then full. That's how it works here."

The cooler dropped a little in Syed's grip. Elyse looked at her phone, at the time, at the lake schedule she'd apparently built in her head without telling him the schedule existed. "The last Saturday of June. That was the plan. I told my cousin we're coming."

"I know."

"You knew when you made the plan?"

"I found out Thursday." The words came out clipped and small. He didn't add that he had made the plan anyway, on Friday, at the fry place, because he had wanted it to be true more than he had wanted to check. He should have said something Thursday night. He let the admission stand there in the driveway with no decoration on it.

Mr. Sánchez, who had been leaning against the garage watching the whole exchange like a man at a tennis match, straightened up. "Lesson's at two," he said to Mason. "You booked the two o'clock, not the noon. I came early because you looked like a kid who'd stall a sedan into a fence if left unsupervised." He glanced at his watch. "So you've got a decision to make about right now, and it isn't about the lake."

Elyse was already halfway back to Syed's brother's car, keys out. Syed hesitated, cooler in both hands, looking between her and Mason.

"We could take the bus," Syed said, to nobody in particular. "It's four transfers. My brother did it last year, it took all day, but they did it."

Mason got out of the sedan and stood on the warm concrete. "Wait," he said. "Saturday I can't drive you. That part's fixed. But the bus goes either way, and if you're still doing the lake in July, I'll have my hours logged by then, and Elyse's cousin can ride with her parents like they offered." He paused. "I'm not sure the second part works yet. I'm sure about the first part."

Elyse stopped with one hand on the car door. She looked at him for a long second, and the anger in her face loosened into something more tired and more forgiving, though she didn't allay it with words or say it was fine. "Four transfers," she said. "You're buying the coffee at transfer three."

"Done," said Mason.

Syed hoisted the cooler back toward the trunk. "Get in the car, Elyse. We're going to be late and it's not even his fault." He said it loudly enough for Mason to hear, which was the closest thing to a pardon on offer.

Mr. Sánchez walked back toward the sedan and rapped the roof twice. "Two o'clock," he said. "Mirror, signal, shoulder check."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it acts mainly as a feedback: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like carbon dioxide.
story:
Ms. Rahimi had taped the graph to the whiteboard at the front of Room 114, and Austin copied its jagged line into his notebook for the third time, trying to make his hand reproduce the slow climb and the steep, almost vertical turn at the right edge. Fifty years, then a hundred, the axis marching left to right, and the line going up the whole way, gently at first, like a path through sedimentary hills, and then not gently at all. His pencil kept slipping at the steep part. Around him the debate team dragged chairs into their usual crooked circle, and Gabryel arrived last, dropping a folder of printouts on the desk with the confidence of someone who believed folders won arguments.

"Resolution for Saturday," Ms. Rahimi said. "Human activity is the primary driver of recent climate change. Austin, you're affirmative. Gabryel, you're negative. Juan, you judge the round." She tapped the graph. "Austin, before we start, tell me what this shows."

Austin stood, notebook against his hip, and looked at the line he had copied. "Carbon dioxide over the last century," he said. "Parts per million on the vertical axis. It rises the whole time, but the slope isn't constant. The last few decades, it climbs faster. Like the graph itself is losing patience." He heard Juan exhale a small laugh, and it steadied him.

"Solid reading," Ms. Rahimi said. "Now use it. Round starts in five minutes."

Gabryel opened with the folder. He read a line about how water vapor accounts for more of the atmosphere's heat trapping than anything else, then another line about how carbon dioxide was only a trace gas, so thin you could barely find it, and he laid the pages flat with a flourish, as though the paper itself were evidence. "The real cause of warming is water vapor," he said. "Not carbon dioxide. The affirmative's whole graph is a sideshow."

Austin looked down at his notebook and felt the floor tilt slightly under his certainty. He had spent two evenings with the graph and the greenhouse explanation, and Gabryel's attack landed somewhere he hadn't reinforced. Behind him, Juan leaned forward, chin on his fist, waiting, which was worse than a rebuttal, because it meant the gap was visible. Austin's mind went briefly, uselessly, to the idea of the atmosphere as something with a kind of sentience, aware of them, deciding things, and he pushed the image away, because it wouldn't argue back. He needed a distinction, and he could feel its shape without seeing it yet.

"Can I ask you something?" Austin said. "When air gets warmer, what happens to the water vapor in it?"

Gabryel flipped a page, then another, buying time. "There's more of it, I guess. Warm air holds more."

"Right." Austin drew two quick arrows in his margin, one short, one long, feeding into the first. "So water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas. I'll give you that, it's in your own source. But it's not the thing that starts the warming. It responds to warming. Other gases, like carbon dioxide, raise the temperature first, and then the warmer air holds more water vapor, and that extra vapor traps more heat. The carbon dioxide starts it. The water vapor amplifies it."

Juan's pen stopped moving. "So what's that called," he said, "when one thing's output feeds back into itself like that?"

"A feedback," Austin said. "Water vapor acts mainly as a feedback."

Gabryel was quiet for a moment, and Austin watched him reread his own printouts, and he recognized the expression, because he'd worn it an hour ago over his own notes: the look of someone discovering that a source had told him less than he'd heard. Gabryel was not a cheat; he was fast, and fast readers skim the load-bearing sentence. "Say the last part again," Gabryel said, and Austin said it slower: warming started by other gases, like carbon dioxide, amplified by water vapor the warmer air holds. Gabryel wrote it down in the margin of his own evidence, in small careful letters, then looked up almost gratefully. "Okay. That's actually the better argument for my side anyway. I just need to restructure."

Ms. Rahibi had been silent the whole exchange, arms folded, and now she said, "Time," which meant something different than a clock. She pointed at Austin. "What's still uncertain for you? A debater who claims certainty on everything loses to a careful one."

Austin looked at the graph again, at the copied line in his notebook with its smeared steep section. "I can read the line," he said. "I can explain the mechanism. What I can't do from this graph alone is tell you exactly how much of the warming is ours and how much is everything else, because that's a judgment about attribution, not a measurement sitting in front of me. I'd rather say that than pretend the graph answers it by itself." He glanced at Gabryel. "And he wasn't wrong that water vapor matters most by amount. He was wrong about what that means. Those aren't the same mistake, and I don't want to make the second one while correcting the first."

"Cross-examination," Juan said, grinning, standing to play examiner now that the round had dissolved into something better than a round. "First question. If the world got cooler tomorrow, what would the water vapor do?"

Gabryel pulled his chair around so the three desks touched, and Austin set his notebook flat in the middle where both of them could see the two arrows and the steep, imperfect line.

"Shrink with it," Austin said. "Same logic, other direction. Now ask me something hard."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries.
story:
The new warm-up appeared on the first Tuesday of pre-season, printed on a sheet of paper that Mr. Bui taped to the chain-link fence behind the far goal. It had diagrams. Little stick figures with arrows at their knees, feet splayed, arms out for balance, and beside them words like "single-leg hop" and "nordic hamstring" in a font that looked borrowed from a science textbook. Hailey read it twice while the rest of the team dropped their bags in a line along the fence and pretended not to be reading it at all.

"This is a warm-up," Charlene said, holding one of the diagrams up to the gray sky as though light might improve it. "It's a punishment with stretches." The field sat at the edge of their littoral town, flat and salt-scoured, gulls wheeling over the canteen, and the wind off the water flipped the pages so that Charlene had to pin one against her thigh. She was funny about it, and the laughter moved down the line of players like weather, but Hailey noticed she kept the page.

They had reason to be suspicious. The season before, Ludovic had planted his foot to cut left, and his knee had gone one way while the rest of him went another, and the sound had carried across the pitch. He was back now, brace strapped on, cleared in June, but he warmed up apart from everyone, private and slow, and when Mr. Bui asked him to demonstrate a landing drill, Ludovic's face did something complicated before he agreed. Some of the parents imputed the injury to the turf, which they'd complained about for years, and some to bad luck, which required nothing of anyone.

Hailey did the drills. Not out of virtue; she simply found that if she did them, the grumbling flowed around her, and she could think. But she wanted to know what the sheet actually was, because "neuromuscular" was a word the diagrams never explained. On Thursday she stayed after practice, ostensibly collecting cones, and asked Mr. Bui where it came from. He didn't lecture. He pulled a folded study from the gear bag, handed it over, and said only, "Page two," before walking off to argue with a gull that had taken over the canteen roof.

She read it under the floodlight while the moths battered the housing above her. The program was called a neuromuscular warm-up, and it trained balance, landing and cutting technique. It had been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries. That was it. No promise, no guarantee, only a reduction in risk, phrased with the dull honesty of people who counted things carefully. She read it again at the bus stop, and a third time on the bus, where a man beside her glanced over and visibly decided she was studying for something medical.

"Did you know," she said at practice the next week, jogging beside Charlene during the balance sequence, arms out, wobbling on one leg like everyone else, "this isn't just fitness nonsense. It's the landing and cutting part. That's what it's for." Charlene hopped, landed soft, and considered. "So all the hopping we're doing," she said, "the hopping is the point." Ludovic, a few feet ahead, didn't turn around, but his stride changed, and afterward he asked to borrow the study, and kept it for a week, and returned it with the corners soft from handling.

Hailey's own position assembled itself slowly, the way the drills themselves were supposed to assemble in your body. She believed the numbers; she'd read them herself, and she liked that they didn't promise safety, only lowered odds, which felt like the truth. But she also understood the team's resistance, because the drills were tedious and unglamorous and the season was short. Her father had an adage about not fixing what wasn't broken, and she caught herself halfway between that and the folded study in her bag, holding both, unable to make them agree.

She settled on doing them regardless, and on saying why when anyone asked, and on admitting, when Charlene pressed her on the bus home, that she couldn't be certain it would matter for any one of them on any one cut. "The risk goes down," Hailey said. "It doesn't go away." Charlene nodded out the window at the harbor, the water going pewter in the late light, and then said, "You're very comforting, has anyone ever told you that," and Hailey laughed, and beneath the laughter her knees kept doing the small quiet work of landing well, hop after hop, all the way down the shore road.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration states that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures.
story:
Mr. Hoffmann arranged the desks into a horseshoe before the bell, which meant the debate was real, graded, and unavoidable. He dropped a photocopied article in front of each of them: a county in the next state had approved a new pesticide for its soybean fields, and a citizens' group was suing to block it. "Resolved," he wrote on the board, "that the county should suspend use of the pesticide until harm is proven." Angel would argue for the suspension. Jazlyn would argue against. The rest of them would have to choose, out loud, by the end of the period.

Alyssa had spent two evenings in the library with the article and her notebook, and she still had no position, which frightened her more than the debate itself. The pesticide was called Atraxin. Preliminary studies showed elevated nitrates in two watersheds near test fields and a possible decline in a native pollinator, but the word possible appeared so many times it started to look like a hedge. Angel's argument wrote itself: two watersheds, a dying pollinator, wait, see, protect. Jazlyn's argument was harder and more interesting: the county's farmers were losing twenty percent of their yield to a resistant pest, and Atraxin was the only cost-effective option. Jazlyn had grown up on a farm. She said the word yield the way other people said the word rent.

When the bell rang, Angel opened by excoriating the county board for treating an entire watershed as a testing laboratory, and she was good at it, her voice rising until the classroom felt warmer. "We don't drink possibly," she said. "We don't drink preliminary." Jazlyn was reticent by comparison, almost quiet, and it worked against expectation; she laid out the numbers, the farmers' margins, the loans. "You want them to wait for proof," she said. "While they wait, they lose the farm. That's the trade-off. Somebody pays either way."

Mr. Hoffmann, who had said almost nothing, wrote a word on the board and did not turn around. Precautionary principle. "Somebody in this room has encountered this before," he said. "Not me explaining it. You."

Alyssa's stomach dropped, because she had. Three nights earlier, unable to sleep, she had gone past the article into the library's database and found a United Nations document from 1992, the Rio Declaration on environment and development. She had read Principle 15 twice, then copied it into her notebook word for word: where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation. She had underlined irreversible. She had underlined certainty. It had felt like finding a door in a wall she'd been pushing on.

She raised her hand. "Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration," she said, and the room shifted, the way it does when someone brings in something from outside. She read it from her notebook. "It means the burden flips. If the damage might be serious or irreversible, you don't wait for full scientific certainty before you take cost-effective preventive measures. Waiting is itself a decision. It's not neutral." Jazlyn turned in her seat and looked at her for a long moment, and Alyssa understood that she had just done something to a friendship, though she couldn't yet say what.

"That's a UN document," Jazlyn said finally. "Soft law. Aspirational."

"It's still the standard they wrote down," Alyssa said. "For the whole world. In 1992."

The debate went on without her for a while. Angel pushed on unintended consequences, how a ban could push farmers to an older, dirtier chemical, and how do you ban one thing without knowing what replaces it. Someone compared the farmers to epicures, willing to let the environment pay for their comfort, which was unfair, and Alyssa said so, and the room laughed at the word, and she felt the strange pleasure of holding a position, even a temporary one. She argued the principle. She conceded the trade-off. She said, twice, that she wasn't sure the pollinator data was strong enough, and twice that it might not need to be.

Then Mr. Hoffmann asked for the vote, and here Alyssa slowed down inside, because she had realized something on the walk to this class that she had not told anyone. Her father, who traveled most springs selling crop inputs to cooperatives across three states, had left a brochure on the kitchen counter last week. Atraxin was his company's product. His commission depended on the counties that adopted it. He had not known, when she chose the topic, that she would find it; she had not known, when she found it, that it was his.

The vote came to her last. Angel had nine for suspension. Jazlyn had six against. Four had abstained, hiding behind uncertainty, the exact thing the principle was written to forbid. Alyssa thought of her father at the counter, buttering toast, saying the season looked good. She thought of the word irreversible, which applies to watersheds and also, she was beginning to see, to other things. She said, "For suspension," and heard Angel exhale.

After the bell, Jazlyn gathered her books without looking at her, and Mr. Hoffmann said, quietly, "Interesting that you abstained from telling us the whole context." Alyssa asked what he meant. He turned the county article over, and there in the masthead, small, was the name of the pilot program's sponsor: her father's company, which had also, she now saw, funded the preliminary studies. Both studies. The ones showing possible harm, and the ones showing none. She picked up her notebook, with the principle copied into it, and went to find a phone.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In 2025, US union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404, compared with $1,174 for workers who were not union members, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
story:
Mr. Bakker had left the blinds half open, and the light on the whiteboard cut through the word INDUSTRIALIZATION in faded blue marker, a lesson from two weeks ago that nobody had wiped away. Felix sat near the window with his application for Harmon's Grocery folded in his back pocket, the shift schedule already stapled to it. He had not told his father he was applying. His father had opinions about unions the way some people had opinions about weather, loudly and without any expectation of being able to change it.

Mr. Bakter wrote a date on the board and turned around. "Today we're doing labour history, which some of you will find boring and some of you will find personally relevant in about four months." A few people laughed. Felix did not, because four months was exactly right.

At lunch, in the corner of the cafeteria with the wobbly table, Mckinley slid his phone across to Serena. On the screen was a photo of his paycheck stub from Voss Foods, where he'd been stocking shelves since March. Serena worked at Kessler's, the other grocery chain across town, and she pulled out her own stub and laid it beside his like they were comparing hands of cards.

"Wait," Mckinley said. "You're making how much an hour?"

"Twenty-two fifty. You?"

"Eighteen." He picked up the phone again, squinting at it as if the number might rearrange itself. "I've been there longer than you've been at Kessler's. I trained two new guys last month."

Serena tapped the edge of her stub, where a small line read UNION DUES. "Mine takes a bit out for dues. It's still not close." She said it without triumph, the way you'd report a score in a game neither of you had chosen the teams for.

Felix had Harmon's application in his hand now, though he didn't remember taking it out of his pocket. "Which one is Harmon's? Is it like yours or like his?"

"Neither, I think," Serena said. "Non-union, but they start you at nineteen." She paused. "My cousin looked all this up when I got hired. In 2025, union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404, compared with $1,174 for workers who were not union members. Bureau of Labor Statistics. She made me memorize it like it was going to be on a test."

Mckinley leaned back. "Median. So that's the middle, not the average."

"Middle," Serena confirmed. "Half above, half below."

In fifth period the classroom had gone soft and turbid with afternoon heat, the air thick enough that the map of the Ruhr valley on the wall seemed to be sinking into it. Mr. Bakker was talking about the eight-hour day, about how it had not been given but taken, and Felix found himself writing in the margin of his notes, not facts, but a small ledger: Harmon's, nineteen an hour, no dues, no vote. Kessler's, if they'd even hire him, twenty-two fifty and a card. He thought about his father's voice saying the word "union" the way he said the word "bureaucracy," and about Mckinley's face over the paycheck, and he understood, slowly, that these were two different accounts of the same world, and that both men believed theirs completely.

He stayed after the bell. "Mr. Bakker. Quick question, not for the test."

Mr. Bakker erased the board in long strokes. "Those are the only good questions."

"If a place isn't unionized, and you take the job anyway, are you part of the problem? Or is that just, like, surviving?"

Mr. Bakker considered him for a moment. "That's a question people died arguing about, in the era we're studying. I'm not going to settle it in one hallway conversation. But I'll say this: the people in my chapter didn't wait until the question was settled to act." He set the eraser down. "Also, Kessler's hires in the summer. Serena could introduce you."

That evening Felix filled out the Kessler's application at the kitchen table while his father watched television in the next room. His father came in for a glass of water, saw the logo at the top of the page, and stopped.

"Kessler's," his father said. "They're organized."

"I know."

His father stood there for a while, water glass in hand, the refrigerator humming behind him. "My father would have liked that," he said finally, which was not the opinion Felix had been bracing for, and which he could not entirely transliterate into anything he understood about his grandfather, a man who existed for him mostly as a photograph in a toolbox. His father went back to the television without another word.

Felix wrote his name at the bottom of the application, dated it, and texted Serena: "Do you work Saturday? I could drop it off and you could show me where the time clock is."

Her reply came in under a minute. "Noon shift. Wear the ugly vest if they give you one. Mckinley's applying too."

Felix set the phone face down on the table, folded the application into thirds, and put it in his back pocket where the Harmon's one had been.

"Wear the vest," he said to the empty kitchen.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
Vanessa would like it entered into the record, first of all, that she did not care about singing the Four Questions this year. Not even a little. She was sixteen. She had a chemistry test on Tuesday and a pair of tights that had already betrayed her twice. The last thing she wanted was to stand up in front of eighty people at the community hall and chant in Hebrew, which is why she had been practicing in the shower all week, quietly, so nobody would get ideas.

The hall smelled like chicken soup and floor wax, and Mr. Munro, the caretaker, was unfolding the last of the rented tables with the grim satisfaction of a man who had fought this exact battle for thirty years. "Your grandmother," he told Vanessa, apropos of nothing, "has opinions about my chairs." She did. Her grandmother had vitriolic opinions about many things, including store-bought charoset, which she called "a dishonor to apples everywhere," and she had brought her own in a Tupperware the size of a car tire.

Vanessa's job, as the youngest cousin on her side, had always been the Four Questions. She knew them cold. Then the Friedmans arrived, and with them Layan, age seven, clutching a Haggadot upside down. Layan was the daughter of Vanessa's mother's oldest friend, which in practice meant she was Vanessa's responsibility the moment she walked through the door. Her parents were immediately absorbed into a dispute about parking. Layan stood there like a small, solemn paperweight.

"Vanessa," her grandmother said, in the voice of someone delivering wonderful news, "isn't Layan the youngest child here?" She said it brightly, the way you'd announce a raffle win. Vanessa said, "Sure," in a voice that was absolutely fine, and went to help Mr. Munro with the chairs, which did not need help, and were fine, and so was she.

It was Gavyn, her grade 12 cousin, who intercepted her by the coat rack. He had the loose, amused posture of a boy who had recently discovered that being taller than everyone was a personality. "You're doing the face," he said.

"I'm not doing a face. I'm doing coats."

"You're doing the face you did when your aunt brought a date to Hanukkah." He nodded across the hall, where Layan had been installed at the kids' table with a plate of parsley and a look of mounting dread. "She's terrified, by the way. Her mom says she's been whispering the first line to the bathroom mirror all week."

"Then she's prepared," said Vanessa, hanging a coat with unnecessary force.

Layan, it turned out, was not prepared. When Vanessa went over to drop off a cup of grape juice, which extruded from the urn's spigot in a thin purple ribbon that missed the cup entirely and puddled on the table, the little girl looked up and said, "I can't do it. I'm going to say it wrong and everyone will look at me."

Vanessa knew exactly zero ways to answer this that weren't lies, because everyone would look at her, and saying it wrong was in fact a live possibility, and Vanessa herself had once sung a whole verse in the wrong order at age nine and her uncle Yonatan still brought it up at Purim. So she did the only honest thing and sat down. "Everyone's going to look at you," she agreed. "They look at whoever asks the questions. That's the whole deal."

Gavyn materialized with his chair and a plate he had clearly built for sharing. "Okay, rookie," he said to Layan, and then, to the table at large, "announce your furlough from snacks of any leavened description, people, I'm in coaching mode." He flipped Layan's Haggadot right side up. "You're the youngest, so the questions are yours. That's the custom, youngest asks. And you start with the big one." He cleared his throat with theatrical gravity. "Why is this night different from all other nights?"

"Why is this night different from all other nights," Layan repeated, flat as a parking lot.

"There's a tune," Vanessa said, before she could stop herself, and hummed the first phrase. She had not planned to say that. She had, in fact, spent the last hour strenuously not saying that.

They drilled it through the appetizer course. Gavyn conducted with a celery stalk. When Layan got the whole first question out in one breath, he awarded her the celery, which she accepted like a medal. Between repetitions, Layan asked Vanessa, "Do you know them all?" and Vanessa said, "Yeah," and Layan said, "Then why is it mine?" and Vanessa opened her mouth and found nothing in it, because the true answer was "Because you're the youngest and that's the custom," and the other true answer, the one sitting underneath, was something she was still deciding whether to look at directly. It was possible, she thought, to be genuinely glad for someone and also a small amount gutted, both at once, without either one cancelling the other out. She wasn't sure. She filed it next to the chemistry test.

When Mr. Munro dimmed the lights for the candle blessing, Layan's hand found Vanessa's under the table and gripped it like a handlebar. Then the blessing was done, and the room turned toward the kids' table, all eighty faces, exactly as promised, and Layan stood up on her chair, which nobody had authorized, and sang.

"Why is this night different from all other nights?"

Her voice cracked on the second word and recovered. Somewhere behind Vanessa, her uncle Yonatan was already whispering about the time she did the verses out of order. Vanessa squeezed the small hand once and did not turn around.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, which did not reveal that its author was a woman.
story:
Cole found the book behind the returns cart, an old edition of Jane Eyre with a cracked spine and a date stamp reading 1989, and he opened it to the title page mostly out of boredom. "By Currer Bell," it said. He sat down at one of the long tables near the windows and stared at the name, because Mr. Flores had assigned them a paper on the novel and had never once mentioned anyone called Currer.

He was supposed to be applying a critical lens, feminist or Marxist, his choice, and so far his choice had produced three crossed-out paragraphs about a governess named Jane and a man named Rochester who kept his first wife in an attic. Cole had understood the plot. What he had not understood was what he was supposed to do with it. Justus, two seats down, was highlighting the same chapter in three colors, which made Cole feel worse.

"Who's Currer Bell?" Cole asked.

Justus leaned over, looked at the title page, and shrugged. "Some editor? A translator?"

They pulled the library's reference volume down together, the fat one about nineteenth-century authors, and Cole ran his finger down the column until he found it. Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, a pen name that did not reveal its author was a woman. He read the line twice. "So the book everybody made us read," he said slowly, "came out with a man's name on it. On purpose."

Justus said nothing for a moment, and Cole watched him do the same arithmetic he was doing: a woman writing in 1847, choosing a mask so the book would be read at all. Then all at once the lens made sense, or started to. It wasn't a machine you pointed at a book. It was a question. Who had power, who was paid, who had to hide to be heard. Jane was a governess, dependent on wages, and Rochester owned the house. Cole looked at his crossed-out paragraphs and thought he might actually be able to write this now, though he still wasn't sure whether Brontë was exposing that world or just surviving it, and he was honest enough with himself to know he might not decide by Friday.

Frederique arrived at four with her own stack of books and a problem of her own. She wanted the corner table by the biography shelf, the one with the good lamp, because she had a scholarship interview on Saturday and she had decided, sometime between third period and now, that she needed to be able to say something intelligent about Victorian women writers. She had heard Cole say "Currer Bell" from halfway across the room, which stopped her mid-search.

"That's my interview topic," she said. "Sort of. Did you know she used a man's name?"

"Just found out," Cole said. "In the reference book. It's in there." He slid the volume toward her, and she sat down without asking, taking the seat Justus had left empty when he wandered off toward the periodicals.

Frederique turned the pages carefully, as if the fact might be fragile. Charlotte Brontë, 1847, Currer Bell. She had known some of it, vaguely, the way you know a rumor, but seeing it in print made it solid, something she could carry into a room full of adults on Saturday. She was quiet, and Cole watched her hold the page open with one finger. He wondered whether she was relieved that a person could hide like that and still get read, or whether it made her angry, or whether it was both at once, the way his own reaction seemed to be both at once.

"How did anyone find out it was her?" Cole asked.

"People guessed," Frederique said. "Then she and her sisters admitted it, sort of. It's in the letters." She tapped the page. "You can use this, you know. For your paper. If Jane Eyre was published under a man's name, then every time Jane talks about wanting work and respect, there's a real woman standing behind it who couldn't sign her own name."

Cole wrote that down, word for word, and then crossed out half of it because it sounded better in her voice than it would in his. He thought about asking whether that made Brontë a feminist or whether the word didn't exist yet in the way they used it, but he didn't want the answer decided for him before he'd worked out what he thought. That was the strange part, he noticed: the lens was supposed to settle things, and instead it had opened them.

"Justus," he called toward the periodicals, "get your highlighters and come look at this."

Justus came back with a magazine he hadn't paid any attention to, dropped it on the table, and leaned over the old title page again. "Currer Bell," he read aloud. "So she had to lie to tell the truth."

"That's one way to put it," Cole said, and pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward him.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: Historian Frances Wood argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China, pointing out that his book never mentions tea, foot-binding or the Great Wall.
story:
The archive smelled like pencil shavings and radiators, which was not what Ryder had expected of a place that kept four hundred years of paper alive. He had come for a report on Marco Polo, assigned by a teacher who wanted "primary sources or nothing," and he'd brought his laptop, a granola bar, and the confidence of a boy who had read the first three paragraphs of a Wikipedia article at eleven the night before. The reading room had eight long tables, one other visitor, and a woman behind the desk whose badge said Ms. Morin.

"I need sources on Marco Polo," he said. "Like, his actual journey."

Ms. Morin looked at him over her glasses the way someone looks at a bird that has flown into the house. "Which journey? The one he took, or the one he wrote down?"

Ryder blinked. "Aren't they the same thing?"

She led him into the stacks without answering, which he was beginning to understand was her way of answering. She pulled a translation of The Travels, then a slim modern book with a plain cover, and set them side by side on a table like two witnesses who had not yet seen each other. "Start with the argument between them," she said. "Arguments are where the interesting history lives."

He opened the slim book first, because it was shorter, and that was how he learned that a historian named Frances Wood had argued that Marco Polo might never have reached China at all. Ryder read the sentence twice, then a third time, feeling something tip over in his head. Wood's evidence was almost insultingly simple: Polo's book never mentions tea. It never mentions foot-binding. It never mentions the Great Wall. Ryder sat back. He had been to school presentations about the Great Wall. Everyone had. How could a man live in China for years and not once mention the Great Wall?

He texted Puneet, who was doing a report on the Silk Road two tables of history away. "did you know some historian thinks marco polo made the whole china thing up? frances wood. he never mentions tea. TEA."

Puneet's reply arrived in bursts, the way Puneet did everything: "what." Then: "that's like going to paris and not mentioning the eiffel tower." Then, after a pause: "wait bad example. was the tower even built then. this is why I hate history. everything is a maybe."

Ryder grinned at his phone, then felt vaguely guilty and put it away. He opened the translation of The Travels and started hunting, the way you hunt for your name in a class list. Tea. Foot-binding. Wall. He found customs and khan and silver and battle, but the words he wanted did not surface, and after forty minutes he had a page of things Polo did mention, which was enormous, and a much shorter page of things he didn't. Neither page told him anything on its own. That was the part that kept snagging him. Two lists, both true, pointing in opposite directions.

There was a folder of teaching materials in the archive's education collection, left there by a retired teacher, and inside it Ryder found a photocopy of a letter a student had written to a museum in 1998, asking about exactly his question. The letter was handwritten and completely serious, which made it funnier. "Dear Sir or Madam," it began. "I have heard that Marco Polo may not have gone to China because he does not mention the Great Wall, foot-binding, or tea. My grandfather says this proves nothing because he has been to Florida four times and never once mentioned Disney World, and he loved it. Please advise." Ryder laughed out loud, then covered his mouth, and Ms. Morin glanced over with an expression that was either disapproval or approval, he genuinely could not tell. Attached to the letter was the museum's reply, polite and careful, explaining that historians disagreed, that some things a traveler would assume his readers already knew, and that absence of evidence was a tricky thing to build a case on.

Ryder copied both lists and the letter and spread them out. Puneet appeared at his elbow, chair scraping, uninvited. "Charley says foot-binding was happening way before Polo, so he would've seen it," Puneet reported, having apparently convened a summit in the cafeteria without him. "Also Charley says tea was everywhere, like water. So either Polo went and had the worst memory in Venice, or he stayed home and made it all up from other travelers' stories."

"Or both lists are wrong," Ryder said slowly, surprising himself. "Maybe tea and foot-binding were so ordinary to him that writing them down would've been gratuitous, like me writing a report about my house and mentioning that we have a fridge."

Puneet considered this. "Then why go at all? If the ordinary stuff vanishes because it's ordinary, how does anyone know anything?"

"That's the actual question," Ryder said. "Not whether he went. It's why we keep asking, and why the answers change. Wood asked about tea because she was living now, reading now. Someone in 1898 might not have ever thought to check for tea, because they didn't ask the same questions."

He wrote that in his notebook and then stopped, because he wasn't sure it was true, only that it felt true, and he underlined it anyway with a small warning question mark beside it, the way Ms. Morin had put question marks in the margins of the museum's reply. He wondered whether the report could hold all of this at once: a man who might have gone, might not have, a book full of everything except the three things a modern reader looks for first, and a grandfather in Florida refusing to mention Disney World. He thought about how a source written under the duress of a prison editor, or shaped by a scribe who wanted a good story, might drop things without anyone deciding to drop them. History, he was starting to suspect, was less a record and more an argument that never fully recuperates from its own gaps.

Ms. Morin passed by on her rounds and paused at his spread of papers. "Found your journey?"

"Found about four of them," Ryder said. "They don't agree with each other."

"Good," she said. "Come back when they do, and I'll retire."

He stayed until the radiators clicked off, photocopying the letter, because the grandfather argument had to go in the report, footnotes and all. At the front desk he checked out the Frances Wood book, and Ms. Morin stamped the card and slid it across, and Ryder noticed she had added, in the margin of his own notebook while he wasn't looking, a single neat question mark.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data.
story:
Luca had been sitting on the end of the bench for eleven minutes of game time, which was long enough to count the screws in the scoring table, when Matheo leaned over during a timeout and said, "You're the one who reads. Tell Coach the hot hand is real."

The gym smelled like floor wax and the popcorn nobody was selling in the third quarter of a Tuesday game. Luca looked at Matheo, then at the whiteboard, where Ms. Gallagher, who coached physics in the afternoons and this team in the evenings, was drawing an arrow toward the elbow. She was saying something about shot selection, about not forcing it when the first one doesn't fall.

"He doesn't believe in it," Matheo said. "He told Louis yesterday that streaks are a myth. He said some study from the eighties proved it." Matheo had made five three-pointers in a row at the end of the last practice, and everyone had seen it, and Coach had still put him on the bench for the second half tonight. "Five in a row, Luca. You saw it."

"I saw it," Luca said, although what he had actually seen was more complicated than that. He had seen the first two go in and the last three get taken with a confidence that looked different from the way Matheo usually shot, a taller release, a stiller head. Or maybe he had only decided afterward that he had seen that. That was the problem, and it had been bothering him since Louis brought it up in study hall last week, the way questions do when they refuse to stay in the classroom.

Louis, who kept a spreadsheet of every shot the team had taken all season, angle and distance and result, had commandeered the argument immediately. "The eighties study is the famous one," he had said, tapping his laptop. "Everyone cites it. But I read that in 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias, and they found evidence of streak shooting in the same data." He said it twice that week, once in study hall and once on the bus, as if repetition might make Coach hear it.

So when the timeout ended and Ms. Gallagher looked down the bench, and Matheo shot Luca a glance that was half plea and half dare, Luca stood up and followed her to the huddle. "Coach. One thing. Louis found something. The study that said streaks aren't real, the 1985 one, it had a flaw. Two economists, Miller and Sanjurjo, in 2018, showed the analysis was biased, and they found evidence of streak shooting in the same data. Same data. It was there the whole time."

Ms. Gallagher studied him the way she studied a failed lab, with interest rather than anger. "The same data," she repeated. She looked at Matheo, then at the clock, then back at Luca. Down the floor, the other team's point guard dribbled in place, waiting, impatient with other people's ideas.

"Here's my problem," she said quietly, so only the huddle could hear. "If I put him in and he's not hot, I've benched Devin for nothing. If I leave him out and he was hot, I've wasted it. Either way I'm guessing." She paused. "But a pragmatist takes the shot that's supported by the best evidence, even when the best evidence is new. Fine. Matheo, in. Luca, you tell me at the four-minute mark whether he's still in the streak or just shooting like he always does."

Matheo played the next four minutes like a man trying to prove a theorem. His first three rattled out. His fourth went in clean, off a screen Luca could see he'd been waiting for, a judicious shot, taken in rhythm rather than in desperation. His fifth, from the corner, hit nothing but net. On the bench, Louis leaned over with the spreadsheet open on his phone, recording each one, and Luca found himself watching not just the ball but everything around it, the way Matheo's feet were set a half second earlier than usual, the way he called for the ball instead of waiting for it.

The four-minute mark came with them down six. Luca stood at the scorer's table waiting for the whistle, and he understood suddenly that he had no clean answer to give. Two of the makes had been open looks that any good shooter should hit. One had been contested and gorgeous. Was that a streak, or was it a run of ordinary luck that the mind insists on shaping into a story? Miller and Sanjurjo had found the evidence, and Coach had acted on it, but the evidence lived in data spread over seasons, and Luca had to decide right now, in one dead ball, about one boy on one night.

Ms. Gallagher turned toward the bench and raised one eyebrow at him. Luca put one hand out flat, the universal signal for hold, and Matheo, catching it out of the corner of his eye as he set up for the inbound pass, smiled and said, "Don't you dare."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
The marquee said the horror movie started at 7:40, and Sebastian had been standing under it since 7:15, which he understood was a mistake but could not stop making. He kept checking his phone, then putting it away, then taking it out again as if the time might have changed its mind. When Jaylynn came around the corner from the bus stop, wearing a denim jacket over a band shirt he'd never seen before, he felt something in his chest do a thing he chose not to name.

"You've been here a while," Jaylynn said. "Long enough to memorize every showtime."

"I was being thorough," Sebastian said, and held the door.

He had planned everything, which was its own confession. Tickets bought in advance so neither of them would have to do the awkward reach at the register. Two seats in the middle of the theater, not the back, because the back was for people who knew what they were doing and the front was for no one. He'd read reviews. He'd even read about the movie's jump scares, how many, roughly when, so that nothing on the screen would ambush him the way the whole evening was already ambushing him.

In the lobby, Tyler was working the concession stand, hairnet pushed back like a small dark wave breaking on his forehead. Tyler had been in Sebastian's chemistry class since September, and Tyler's whole manner was to treat every interaction as though the two of you were already deep in an ongoing joke. "Large popcorn," Tyler said when Sebastian ordered. "Smart choice. Sharing popcorn is a documented bonding activity."

"Is that in the curriculum here?"

"Concessions 101." Tyler filled the bag with unnecessary ceremony, then leaned over the counter a little and lowered his voice. "You want my advice, don't do the horror thing on a first date. My cousin did that. Total disaster."

"It's fine," Sebastian said, but the word came out less certain than he'd rehearsed.

They found their seats as the trailers started. Jaylynn put one boot up on the seat in front, then seemed to think better of it, then did it anyway. During the second trailer, Jaylynn leaned over and said, "Okay, honest question. Are you going to be the kind of person who screams, or the kind who pretends they didn't?"

"I'm hoping for a dialectic between the two," Sebastian said. "Screaming, but ironically."

Jaylynn laughed, a short surprised sound, and Sebastian thought: that, at least, was worth the price of the ticket.

The movie was very good at being bad. There was a long hallway, and a sound like breathing coming from inside the walls, and at the thirty-minute mark something happened involving a mirror that made the entire theater gasp at once, a communal intake of breath that Jaylynn later said was her favorite part, the sound of two hundred people losing their dignity together. Sebastian did not scream, exactly, but his hand came down on the armrest and found Jaylynn's hand already there, gripping it, and neither of them moved for the rest of the film. His heart was going like a drum line. He could feel his pulse in his ears.

Afterward, outside under the sodium lights, both of them a little giddy, Jaylynn said, "I can still feel my heart pounding. That's insane. A movie did that."

"I read something," Sebastian said, because he had, three weeks ago, down a late-night rabbit hole about attraction, which itself was telling. "There was this study in 1974. By Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron. Men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge."

Jaylynn looked at him. "Meaning what?"

"Meaning," Sebastian said, "I have no idea if I like you or if that was just a very scary movie."

The honesty of it sat there between them for a second, and then Jaylynn cracked up, hand over mouth, and said, "That is the most Sebastian sentence ever spoken." They started walking, no destination agreed on, past the shuttered bakery and the laundromat with its window full of rotating sheets. Jaylynn said her sister would impugn the whole study, would say a sample of men on a bridge in 1974 told you nothing about anybody, and that her sister was usually right but also completely intransigent about it, which took some of the fun out of agreeing.

"My dad's the opposite," Sebastian said. "He thinks everything is a study of something. Mr. Menon, my neighbor, he says that's just astrology for people with library cards." He liked saying the neighbor's name; it made his life sound populated.

They walked to the bridge over the creek at the end of the shopping center, the pedestrian one, all bolted steel and a slight bounce in the middle that neither of them commented on. In the middle, Jaylynn stopped, hands on the railing. Below, the creek caught the parking lot lights in broken pieces.

"So walk across it," Jaylynn said. "Scary bridge. Then we'll know."

"That's not how it works," Sebastian said. "That's not what the study says at all. It says nothing about the second crossing. Or about you. Or about me, technically, since I'm not the one who's supposed to call an interviewer."

"Then it's not a real experiment," Jaylynn said, and held out a hand, palm up, patient under the streetlight.

Sebastian looked at the hand, then at the far side of the bridge, and thought that whatever was true, it was true on both sides of it. He took the hand and they crossed together, feeling the steel give a little under their steps.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Beyond the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, the Gulf Stream's continuation toward Europe is called the North Atlantic Current or North Atlantic Drift.
story:
The quarry had filled with spring water years ago, and the town had put a chain-link fence around it that everyone climbed anyway. Simon spread the laminated ocean current map on a flat slab of limestone near the edge, weighting the corners with four stones he'd pried loose from the scree. Jude sat across from him with his sneakers hanging over the green water, turning a fishing lure over in his fingers without looking at it.

"Ms. Johansson said I can retake the oceanography unit on Thursday," Simon said. "But I have to explain the Gulf Stream to her, out loud, with the map. Not multiple choice."

Jude's want was simpler and he stated it often: he wanted to catch the bass that lived in the quarry's deep end before his family moved to Ohio in August. He had seen the fish on his phone's sonar app, four shapes holding near the flooded crane. He believed that if he could present a lure at exactly the right depth, drifting it like something carried along, the bass would take it. He talked about currents the way Simon was supposed to talk about them, water moving and carrying things, and Simon had begun to suspect this overlap was not an accident.

He traced the red line with his finger. It ran up the American coast, hugging the shelf, thick and unmistakable, labeled Gulf Stream. Then, past a cluster of shallow marks southeast of Newfoundland, the label changed. The same red line, the same arrow, but now the map read North Atlantic Drift, and in one of Ms. Johansson's handouts it read North Atlantic Current. Simon had lost points on the first test for writing Gulf Stream where the map wanted the other name, and he had argued, and she had marked it wrong twice.

"The map's wrong," Jude said, leaning over to look. "Same line. Why would they rename it?"

"That's what I said. She said the names are real." Simon stared at the shallow marks. He had read the caption under them three times: the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. Beyond the Banks, the red line crossed open water toward Europe, and somewhere in that crossing the name changed over.

Alissa arrived then, coming down the goat path with her backpack on one shoulder and her biology binder under her arm. She was doing an independent project on the quarry's fish, and she sat down next to Simon without being invited. "Speciation," she said, by way of greeting. "Isolated population, no gene flow, new species. The fish in here have been cut off since the forties. I want to prove they're different from the bass in the river."

"You can't prove that with a sonar app," Jude said.

"I can with fin measurements and scale counts. I need fish, though." She looked at his lure. "Alive."

Jude looked at the water. Simon watched them negotiate, Alissa wanting specimens, Jude wanting the catch itself and not the science of it, and he realized he was doing the same thing with the map that they were doing with the fish. Two names for one thing, and the question of whether the names meant two things or one.

He cogitated on it the way his grandfather used that word, slowly, turning the problem like the lure in Jude's fingers. On the first test he had been doctrinaire about it, insisting the map was simply wrong, one current deserved one name, and the insistence had cost him the question and then the argument and then the retake. Now he followed the line past the Banks with his finger and understood it differently. The mapmakers had drawn one line but the naming happened somewhere out there, past the Grand Banks, where the current turned toward Europe.

"So past the Banks, toward Europe, it's called the North Atlantic Current or the North Atlantic Drift," he said, reading the two handouts against each other, one term in each. "Either name. Same water, different name once it's headed for Europe."

"That's stupid," Jude said.

"It's two labels on one line, and both are right. Alissa, is that like your fish? Two names, and whether they're two things depends on where you're standing?"

"Depends on time, not standing," Alissa said. "Which I can't measure yet, because someone won't give me a specimen."

Jude cast. The lure arced out over the deep end and dropped, and he began to reel, slow, letting it swing in the current the wind made on the surface. The line went taut, then tauter, and the rod bent, and Jude stood up so fast he nearly went into the water. Simon grabbed the back of his shirt. Alissa was already unzipping the binder to the page with her measurement table, pen out, and the fish came up green and gold and thrashing against the sky, and the three of them leaned over it together at the quarry's edge.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Concussion guidelines say an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine.
story:
The ball came off Shayna's bat in the third inning of a scoreless game, and Brianna, playing shortstop, dropped her glove a half second late. It caught her above the temple, a flat crack that carried across the diamond. She sat down in the dirt. She did not fall, exactly; she lowered herself the way you do when the ground has become the only reliable thing.

The coach jogged out, and so did Sonya from third. Brianna waved them off before they reached her. "I'm fine," she said. "It clipped me." Her ears were ringing in a small, distant way, like a television left on in another room, and the outfield looked slightly tilted, though when she stared at the fence it straightened itself out.

In the dugout the coach asked her the questions she expected: what inning, what score, who pitched last week. Brianna answered all of them correctly, which she found quietly satisfying, proof of something. "See," she said, pulling her helmet back on. "Put me back in." She had missed most of last season with a wrist injury, and scouts from two colleges had asked about her summer schedule, and this game, against this team, mattered in a way she could not afford to be casual about. The coach looked at Ms. Choi, the volunteer who kept the book and happened to be an ER nurse, and Ms. Choi said nothing, only watched.

From the bench, Shayna watched too. She had known Brianna since they were eleven, had watched her play through a rolled ankle, a jammed thumb, a July game in ninety-six degrees where Brianna refused water between innings because the other pitcher took no water. Shayna admired that and had also begun, this summer, to wonder about it. In May, after a lecture in her health class, she had looked up return-to-play protocols on her phone and read one line that had stayed with her, and she thought of it now with a specific dread. She walked down the fence line until she stood beside the coach.

"Coach, last spring I looked this up after my cousin got hurt at the ice rink," Shayna said, keeping her voice low. "She took a hit and begged to go back out before the final period, and her trainer wouldn't let her. The concussion guidelines say a player with a suspected concussion can't return the same day. Even if they feel fine." She heard how it sounded, like she was quoting a pamphlet at the worst possible moment, but she kept going. "I think we have to hold her out."

The coach's jaw worked. "She answered every question."

"That's not what the guideline is about," Shayna said. "It's the same day. Period."

Brianna, close enough to hear all of it, stood up so fast her helmet clattered off the bench. "I'm right here," she said. "Ask me anything." She recited the date, the opposing pitcher's name, the count when the ball hit her. She felt a thin anger, and beneath the anger something less tenable, a wobble in her own certainty, because the outfield had tilted again on her way over and she had corrected for it without letting anyone see. She had spent her whole athletic life believing that toughness was a math problem: if you could still perform, you were fine. Shayna was offering a different arithmetic, one where feeling fine didn't enter into it at all, and Brianna wanted to argue with it and could not find the argument.

"You're done for today," the coach said finally. "We'll recheck you tomorrow."

Brianna spent the rest of the game on the bench, spikes unlaced, arms folded, hating every inning and also, in a smaller voice she tried to drown out, listening to it. Between the fifth and sixth she leaned toward Shayna. "I'm not saying you were right," she said. "I'm saying if it were Sonya who took that ball, I'd have said exactly what you said. Which is annoying, honestly." Sonya, two seats down, laughed once, then covered it. Shayna didn't proselytize, didn't turn it into a speech about safety; she just bumped Brianna's shoulder with her own and said, "Then we agree on the rule and not on who it applies to."

They lost two to one in the eighth. Afterward, in the parking lot, Brianna sat on the tailgate of her mother's truck while Ms. Choi shone a penlight in her eyes, unhurried, thorough. "You did the right thing sitting," Ms. Choi said, and Brianna, who an hour earlier would have argued, only nodded. The headache had settled in behind her eyes like weather. Her mother asked, quietly, whether she would tell the scout about it. Brianna looked out past the lights at the dark shape of the outfield fence, the same fence that had straightened itself out whenever she stared.

"I don't know yet," she said.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Many ethicists distinguish doing harm from allowing harm, and most people judge causing a harm as worse than failing to prevent an equal harm, though some philosophers reject the distinction.
story:
The seminar met last period on Fridays, in a room with one window that faced the parking lot, and Ms. Aziz had written a single question on the board before anyone arrived: If you can prevent a harm at no cost to yourself, and you don't, are you as bad as the person who caused it?

Jordyn had prepared an answer, three pages of it, because Ms. Aziz graded these seminars and Jordyn needed the grade. She also wanted something less nameable: the feeling, from last Tuesday's dinner, of being the only person at the table making sense. Her father had argued that not warning the neighbor about the loose porch step was just as bad as loosening it yourself. Her mother had said that was absurd. Jordyn had said nothing, which was its own kind of evidence, and the argument had ended with plates being carried to the sink in silence.

Margot wanted the floor first, as she always did, because she was applying early decision to a program that valued "demonstrated reasoning" and she had decided this class was where she would demonstrate it. She stood up before Ms. Aziz had finished taking attendance. "My whole position is predicated on consequences," she said. "If the neighbor breaks her ankle either way, then the two cases are identical. What happens is the same. Anything else is people flattering themselves."

Chase, who sat by the window and rarely spoke, raised his hand halfway, then put it down, then raised it again. "Most ethicists distinguish doing harm from allowing harm," he said. "And most people judge causing a harm as worse than failing to prevent an equal harm." He paused. "Though some philosophers reject the distinction entirely."

Ms. Aziz wrote two columns on the board. "Keep going," she said, and sat down, which was her way of making them do the work.

Jordyn found herself arguing against her own prepared pages. "It can't just be consequences," she said, "because then Margot has to say a person who lets a child drown in a puddle is exactly as bad as a person who holds the child under, if the outcome matches. Almost nobody actually believes that." Margot gave her a scathing look and said that almost nobody believing something was not an argument, and Jordyn conceded the point, which surprised her. "It's evidence about the concept, though," she said. "Maybe the belief tracks something real that the consequences leave out."

It was at this moment that Chase said, quietly, "There's a genus here, right? Harm. And doing and allowing are supposed to be different species of it. But the philosophers who reject the distinction say the split is fake, that the boundary is drawn by things that don't matter, like motion and stillness." He was looking at the parking lot while he said it. Ms. Aziz wrote genus on the board under the question, and drew a line through it.

The twist came when Margot, annoyed at losing the room, turned the discussion into an accusation. "You're very calm about this for someone who let it happen," she said to Chase. "The chem lab. Last month. You were the last one out. The fume hood was left off overnight and the samples degraded and Mr. Herrera's whole demonstration set was ruined. Everyone knows it was after your group." The room went quiet in the specific way rooms go quiet when a private thing becomes public. Chase didn't deny it. He said he hadn't left the hood off, that he had checked it, and then he stopped, and Jordyn watched him stop, and she understood that there was a second sentence he had decided not to say.

"You saw who did," she said. It wasn't a question.

Chase looked at his hands. "I saw Dani reach across to grab her bag and knock the switch with her elbow. On the way out. She didn't notice." He said it flatly, the way people report facts they have been carrying for a month. "I didn't say anything because she'd already had a write-up that semester, and it would have looked deliberate."

Ms. Aziz did not rescue him, which Jordyn had learned was how Ms. Aziz taught. The seminar had twenty minutes left, and the question on the board had stopped being abstract. Jordyn thought of the porch step, and of her own silence at the table, and of the two columns Ms. Aziz had drawn, and she found that her position had rearranged itself without her permission. She had come in believing, with her mother, that failing to prevent was different in kind. She still believed the distinction held, that Chase's silence and Dani's elbow were not the same thing, that most people's judgment about doing and allowing tracked something real. But she also believed now that the distinction did not get Chase off the hook, that the philosophers who rejected it were wrong about the categories and right about the excuse, that you could not predicate your innocence on a technicality of motion.

"Here's where I've landed," she said, and everyone turned, including Chase. "The harm was done by Dani, not by you, and that matters. But you allowed it, knowing, for a month, and that matters too, and I don't think those two things add up the way the columns suggest. They overlap." Margot asked whether that was a position or a refusal to take one, and Jordyn said she genuinely did not know yet, and Ms. Aziz wrote overlap between the columns and underlined it twice.

After the bell, Chase stayed in his seat. Jordyn gathered her three unused pages and put them in her bag, then took them out again and set them on the desk by the recycling bin without dropping them in. "Dani's in my study hall," she said. Chase looked up. "Monday," she said, and pulled the strap of her bag onto her shoulder.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
Sadie set her fork down before her father finished carving the chicken, which he took as rudeness, though it was really the opposite, an attempt at politeness, since she could not eat and say what she had come to say. "I've been thinking about not voting Tuesday," she told the table. "I don't see what one ballot does. Everybody my age says the same thing. Drayden says it's like dropping a grain of sand on a beach."

Her grandmother, phlegmatic through forty years of family dinners, went on spooning rice onto her plate as if the remark were weather. Her father set the knife across the roasting pan. "You want to know where your vote came from?" he said. "You think somebody just handed it to kids for fun?"

"I didn't say handed. I said I don't see the point."

"The point." He wiped his hands on the cloth. "When they lowered the voting age to eighteen, the people pushing for it had a slogan. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote. Because back then, eighteen-year-olds could be drafted and sent to the Vietnam War."

Sadie had not known that. She had assumed the age had always been eighteen, the way she assumed the drinking age had always been twenty-one, laws arriving fully formed, like mountains. Her grandmother looked up at last. "Your grandfather was twenty in 1970," she said. "He used to say it. The slogan, when he was shouting at the television." Then she went back to her rice, having contributed exactly as much as she intended to.

The rest of the dinner circumscribed itself around other subjects, her cousin's job, the gutters, whether the roast was dry, but Sadie kept circling back to the arithmetic of it. Eighteen was old enough to be drafted into a war, and so eighteen became old enough to vote. Which meant the vote had been paid for, in a currency she had never had to think about. It did not follow that one ballot mattered more than a grain of sand. But it followed that skipping it was a strange kind of inheritance, refusing something someone else had gone to trouble to get you.

That night she texted Selena, who had been arguing with her for two weeks about a ballot measure on school funding, Selena for, Sadie leaning against because of a line in the funding formula she distrusted. I read the whole text of the measure, she typed. Twice. I still think the formula part is sloppy. But I'm voting for it anyway, because the alternative is nothing, and nothing is what people who never had the vote got by default. This isn't me agreeing with you. Don't get comfortable. Selena replied with a single exclamation point and then, a minute later, "so you admit I was right." Sadie did not answer that one. She did not admit it. She had decided the vote was not an endorsement of Selena's certainty, only a refusal of her own.

Tuesday morning her father drove her to the polling place in the gymnasium of her old elementary school, and Ms. Dhillon, who had lived three doors down since Sadie was six, was working the check-in table. "First time," Ms. Dhillon said, finding the line with her ruler-straight finger. "It never gets old, this part. You'll see." The booth smelled like pencil shavings and floor wax. The pen was chained to the shelf, which Sadie found quietly funny, a device to prevent theft in a room full of people performing their most lawful act.

She voted. Some choices she made quickly, some slowly, one race she left blank because she genuinely did not know, and she let that stay blank rather than pretend. That was the part she had not been able to explain to Selena: that she wanted her vote to mean only what she actually meant, no more.

Outside, her father was leaning on the car in the cold. "Well," he said. "Feel different?"

She peeled the "I Voted" sticker off her jacket and looked at it, the little flag, the adhesive already losing its grip. "Ask me in four years," she said, and pressed it back down.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Each feature in a GIS layer links to a row in an attribute table, so data such as the number of residents in each building can be totaled for a selected area.
story:
The departures board at Gate 14 kept flipping between DELAYED and a time that no longer made sense, so Maya opened her laptop on her knees and logged into the school's mapping software while Aleena went to buy overpriced coffee. Ms. Vargas had assigned the presentation before they left for the conference, and Maya was supposed to deliver it: a simulated town meeting about the Cedarbrook flood zone, where she would have to stand up, or in this case sit in a plastic airport chair, and tell the council how many people lived in the water's path.

She had the flood layer loaded, a blue wash creeping over the eastern edge of the city like a stain spreading through cloth. She had the housing layer too, each building a small polygon. When she turned them both on, the polygons that sat inside the blue went darker, and she could select them, drawing a lasso around the neighborhood the way her father once lassoed channels on the television, except this lasso actually gathered something.

The problem was the number. She had counted polygons, forty-one buildings, and forty-one was the number she had been rehearsing all morning. Forty-one homes in the flood zone. She said it out loud once, quietly, to test it, and a man two seats down glanced over before returning to his phone.

"Cedarbrook has forty-one houses in it," Aleena said when she came back with two cups, balancing one on the armrest. "That's what you told me on the bus."

Maya was already finding out that it wasn't enough. When she clicked the selection of buildings, a table opened beside the map, and each polygon had its own row, one row per feature, with columns behind it. One of the columns held residents. She had noticed it days ago without understanding what it was for, and now she sat very still, because she could see that each building in the layer linked to a row, and the rows could be added up for the area she'd selected. She highlighted the residents column for her forty-one polygons and let the software total it.

"Two hundred and six," she read.

"You just sat there for a whole minute," Aleena said. "I thought the wifi died."

"Houses aren't people." Maya turned the laptop so Aleena could see the table. "Each building has a row, and the row has the number of residents, so the selected area totals them. The council meeting is about people, not buildings. Forty-one homes, two hundred and six residents."

Lisa arrived from the bookshop with a bag she wouldn't explain, dropped into the chair across from them, and listened while Maya talked faster than she had all week. Lisa had been her main detractor on the project from the start, not cruelly, just persistently, the way Lisa was about everything: she thought mapping software was a fancy way of saying what everyone already knew, that poor neighborhoods flood. "So what did you actually find out," Lisa asked, "that a person from Cedarbrook couldn't tell you for free?"

Maya thought about the summer before, when she was sixteen, sitting on her grandmother's porch during the evacuation that never quite happened, the river rising and then stopping, and the neighbors arguing on the sidewalk about whose street would go first. Her grandmother had said the city would never buy out her block because nobody important lived there, and Maya had thought at the time that this was just an old woman's bitterness. Now she understood it was also a hypothesis, and she had, without meaning to, built the test.

"I can show it," Maya said. "That's the difference. When the city says the flood zone is uninhabited parkland, I can put the housing layer on top and show the buildings inside it.
