When someone says the relocation would only affect a few families, I can select the area and the residents in each building total to two hundred and six people. Grandmother always said they'd disenfranchise her block by calling it empty, and I used to think she was just angry. But I can see the parcels now, and the people attached to them, and whether the money follows the people or just the property lines."

Ms. Vargas came over from the customer service desk with a new boarding time and was, as always, more effusive than the situation warranted, saying the delay was a gift, an extra hour of rehearsal. She asked Maya to run the presentation right there at the gate, and Maya stood up between the rows of chairs with the laptop angled toward Aleena and Lisa, who folded her arms but leaned in anyway.

"Good evening, council members," Maya began, and pointed at the blue wash on the screen. "The flood zone in Cedarbrook contains forty-one buildings. But buildings don't vote, and buildings don't evacuate. Each feature in the flood layer links to a row in an attribute table, and the number of residents in each building can be totaled for the selected area. That total is two hundred and six. If you approve the buyout, that is how many people you are moving." Aleena raised her cup like a gavel and said, "Motion carries," and somewhere behind them the board flipped to a gate change.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The overall equation for aerobic cellular respiration is C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy: glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water.
story:
The garden on Delancey Street held its heat long after the sun had gone behind the water tower, and Alice had spread her biology notes across two upturned crates beside the tomato beds because Ms. Bakker had told her the shed was locked and the benches were for people who were actually gardening. She was gardening, technically. She had watered the tomatoes. Now she was trying to learn, before Thursday, the steps by which a cell takes glucose apart and turns it into ATP, and the diagram in her textbook kept flattening into arrows and nothing else.

Trace arrived first, carrying a paper bag of plums and no textbook at all. He sat down on the edge of the bed, brushing mulch off his jeans, and looked at her pages upside down. "You're still doing that mitochondria thing," he said. "You've been doing it since May."

"I got a 61 on the last test," Alice said. "I need an 80 on this one or I retake the class in summer school, and summer school would circumscribe everything. Work, the trip, all of it." She said it evenly, the way she had practiced saying it, and Trace looked away toward the pond at the low end of the garden, where the duckweed had come in thick and green.

Joaquin came through the gate with his own book bag and an air of having done the reading, which Alice suspected was partly an affectation and partly true, because Joaquin did things like that, arranged himself so that effort looked like ease. He dropped onto the crate across from her and pulled the diagram toward him without asking. "Okay," he said. "Where do you get lost?"

"Everywhere. Glycolysis I can fake. After that it's just arrows."

Ms. Bakker came around the corner of the shed with a coil of hose over her shoulder. She was the one who had given Alice the plot when nobody else wanted the corner by the fence, and she had a way of standing near a conversation without joining it, which Alice had learned to read as permission rather than intrusion. Now she paused at the spigot, listening.

Joaquin tapped the diagram. "Forget the arrows for a second. What goes in, what comes out. Start there."

Alice recited what she had memorized, the way she memorized locker combinations. "Glucose and oxygen go in. Carbon dioxide and water come out, and energy." She said it flat, and Joaquin didn't nod, which annoyed her.

"Don't say it like a password," he said. "Say it like it means something." He picked up a fallen tomato leaf and held it. "Six carbons in the glucose. Where do they go?"

"Out. In the carbon dioxide." She stopped. Across the path, Trace had gone very still, watching the pond, and she understood suddenly that he was not bored, he was listening. He had failed the same test. He had said so once, in the parking lot, and then made a joke about it, and the joke had circumscribed the subject so neatly that no one had raised it again.

Alice exhaled slowly onto her palm, the way she used to fog windows on the bus. "This," she said. "This is the carbon dioxide. Right now. Six of them, some number of them, coming out of me."

"Out of you," Joaquin said, "from the glucose, from whatever you ate. That's the whole equation. Glucose plus six oxygens gives six carbon dioxides, six waters, and energy." He set the leaf down. "The mitochondria are where most of it happens. That's the part the diagram is showing you."

"But where does the glucose actually break apart?" She looked at the arrows again and for the first time they did not flatten. They were a sequence, a staircase, each step small enough to be survivable, and the cell did not tear the glucose apart in one violent motion but walked it down, step by step, paying out energy as it went. She thought of herself that way and then stopped thinking of herself, because that was the mistake she always made, turning biology into a mirror.

Trace spoke without turning from the pond. "So the carbon in my breath," he said, "came from my food. From like, the bread I ate."

"Yeah," Alice said.

"That's weird. That's actually weird." He turned around and there was something unguarded in his face, and Alice understood that the summer school joke had been its own kind of password, and that he had been waiting all June for someone to say the next part out loud.

Ms. Bakker finished with the hose and came over, wiping her hands on her apron. "You three can stay until the gate needs locking," she said. "If you're going to talk over the pond, talk facing it, not with your backs to it. It's not altruistic of me, I just like listening to people figure things out." She picked up the watering can and carried it toward the bean poles.

Alice turned her crate so she faced the water. Trace pulled his chair around. Joaquin laid the diagram flat on the dirt between the three of them, weighted its corners with plums, and said, "Okay, from the top. Glycolysis. What breaks first?"

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Gar Alperovitz argued in Atomic Diplomacy (1965) that the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union.
story:
The Cold War exhibit occupied the museum's third floor, a long room lit by panels of projected maps that shifted from blue to red depending on which decade the visitor stood in. Eric had been there for forty minutes, standing first at the Berlin Wall fragment, then at the case of civil defense pamphlets, and finally in front of a single black-and-white photograph of a mushroom cloud with a caption that gave a date in August 1945 and nothing else. He had two books in his backpack, one by a historian named Gar Alperovitz, the other by a historian who thought Alperovitz was wrong, and a worksheet from Mr. Ma that read, in his cramped handwriting, Where does the evidence actually point? Show me.

Sasha found him at the photograph. "You've been staring at that thing since we got up here," she said. She unwrapped a granola bar even though the sign by the elevator said no food. "Angelique's downstairs buying postcards of tanks, which tells you something about her."

Eric pulled out the worksheet. "Mr. Ma wants us to take two explanations of how the Cold War started and test them. I picked the bombing of Japan. One book says the bombs ended the Second World War. The other one says they started the Cold War."

"That's a real argument? People argue about that?"

"Alperovitz argued in a book called Atomic Diplomacy, published in 1965, that the bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union." Eric said it carefully, the way he had rehearsed it on the bus, because getting it slightly wrong had cost him once already. In class the previous week he had told Mr. Ma that Alperovitz claimed intimidation was the only reason, and Mr. Ma had looked at him for a long moment and said, read it again, Eric, the word is partly, and Eric had gone home and read it again and found that Mr. Ma was right, which was somehow worse than being wrong in the first place.

"So the bombs were the first act of the Cold War," Sasha said. "Not the last act of World War Two. Those are opposites."

They walked to a bench under a timeline that ran the length of the far wall, 1945 at one end, 1991 at the other, each year a small brass tab. Eric opened the Alperovitz book to the pages he had flagged with receipts. "Here's the problem. He has documents. Telegrams, diary entries, meeting minutes. There's a lot of paper. But the other historian, the one who thinks the bombs were about ending the war, has documents too. Casualty projections, invasion plans. Also a lot of paper."

"So it's a tie."

"No." Eric turned the book over in his hands. The cover was soft from rain, warped at one corner. "It's not a tie, it's a question of apportionment. How much of the decision was one thing and how much was the other. A decision can be mostly about ending the war and partly about the Soviets. Alperovitz's word, partly, is doing real work there. If you drop the word, his whole argument gets stronger and less honest at the same time."

Angelique came up the stairs with her postcards, fanned them out on the bench without asking, and sat down. One of them showed a fallout shelter sign, the old yellow-and-black trefoil. "Eric's doing homework at a museum," Sasha said. "On a Saturday."

"Mr. Ma said we had to come to the actual evidence," Eric said. "Not just read about it. The worksheet says the photograph downstairs, the one of the cloud, is an artifact too, not just a picture. I keep going back to it because the caption doesn't say why. It says when and where and how many kilotons, and then it stops. Fifty years of argument and the museum's caption is three lines long."

Angelique picked up the fallout shelter postcard and looked at it. She was the most taciturn of the three of them, and when she finally spoke it was usually because she had decided the sentence was worth the effort. "My grandfather was in the Navy in 1945," she said. "He would say the bomb ended the war and he was glad. He's not going to read Alperovitz."

"That's the part I can't get past," Eric said. "The veterans, the people who were actually there. If the bombs saved lives, you can't exactly exonerate the decision and also call it a Cold War opening move. Except you can, maybe. That's what I'm trying to write. The evidence for ending the war is real. The evidence for intimidating the Soviets is real. Neither book destroys the other, and the ones that try to, the ones that make it all one thing, are the ones Mr. Ma crossed off the reading list first."

They went down to the second floor, where the photograph hung at the end of a corridor between a case of ration books and a case of propaganda posters. The corridor smelled like the dehumidifiers, a dry metallic smell, and somewhere behind the wall a vent clicked on and off. Eric stood in front of the cloud again and took out his phone and photographed the caption, all three lines of it, then photographed the photograph itself.

Sasha leaned in next to him. "So what's your answer going to be?"

"I'm going to say the evidence supports both, in the proportions nobody can fix, and that the honest position is the one that admits what stays uncertain." He put the phone away. "Mr. Ma is going to hate it or love it. Probably both."

Angelique slid the fallout shelter postcard into his jacket pocket without comment. "For your essay," she said, and walked toward the stairs.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Adding lanes to a congested highway often fails to reduce traffic for long, because faster trips attract more driving until the new space fills; this effect is called induced demand.
story:
The library's back room smelled of carpet cleaner and old toner, and Alexander had claimed the table by the outlet an hour ago, spreading out the printed comments from the city council's website like evidence at a trial. On Tuesday night the council would vote on widening Marsh Road, and he was supposed to speak, because his civics class had been assigned the meeting and Ms. Chen had looked straight at him when she said somebody should represent the students. Kaia slid into the chair across from him and dropped her phone face-up on the table, a petition open on the screen.

"Four hundred signatures since Friday," she said. "My mom signed it twice by accident." She turned the phone toward him. "You're speaking for it, right? Please tell me you're for it."

Alexander hesitated, and she saw it, because Kaia had known him since the year their families had shared a driveway.

"I'm still reading," he said. He tapped the stack of printouts. "Everybody at the meeting is going to say the same thing, that the road is a parking lot at five o'clock. It is. I drive it to practice. But then I found this study from a think tank that counted what happened in other cities after they added lanes."

"Which cities?"

"All over. The study found that adding lanes to a congested highway often fails to reduce traffic for long." He flattened the page with his palm. "Faster trips attract more driving until the new space fills. They have a name for it. Induced demand."

"Induced," Kaia repeated, like the word tasted artificial. "So building more road makes more people drive."

"Basically the new capacity disappears into new trips. I didn't believe it either, so I pulled three more sources, and they circumscribe the finding pretty tightly. There are exceptions, but not many, and not on commuter corridors like ours." He slid the page toward her. She read it with her chin propped on her fist, and the window behind her had gone from white to grey while they worked.

Teo arrived late, hair damp, carrying his bike helmet and an iced coffee he was definitely not supposed to have in the library. He dropped into the third chair and read over Kaia's shoulder without asking. "My dad works at the plant off Marsh Road," he said. "He leaves at four to beat it. If the road gets worse, that's forty more minutes of his day, every day, gone."

"It's not going to get better," Alexander said, gentler than the sentence deserved. "That's what I keep circling. It gets worse either way. With the widening, it gets worse more slowly, in a way, and then it catches up. Without it, it's worse now."

"So don't widen it."

"So then what do we do? That's the part nobody in those comments is answering." He reached across and squared the pages, an old habit from the year he'd organized his mother's medical bills after her surgery, when order had been the only thing he could control. "The bus line out there runs twice a day. The plant shift doesn't match it. There's no safe bike route past the interchange. The road is the whole system right now, and the system is what's broken, not the number of lanes."

Teo gave him a sardonic look over the rim of his cup. "That'll play great with the council. 'The system is broken.' Two minutes per speaker."

Kaia had gone quiet, scrolling through her petition. Alexander watched her thumb slow, stop. "My mom takes Marsh Road to her cleaning jobs," she said finally. "She can't move closer, the rents near the county line are the only ones she can touch. If the road fills up again, they'll just be late, and late means a client drops her." She looked up. "So the people who most need the road fixed are the ones who can't leave it."

The librarian passed their table with a cart of returns and gave the iced coffee a long, deliberate glance, and Teo slid it into his backpack without breaking eye contact with the petition. Alexander pulled a blank sheet toward himself and wrote two headings, lanes and everything else, and under the second one started listing: bus frequency, plant shift times, the interchange, the rent gradient Kaia had just described without naming it. The page filled fast. It was not an argument yet. It was an encapsulation of the whole problem, small enough to hold in one hand, which he found both comforting and slightly dishonest, because the problem was not small and could not be held.

"Okay," Kaia said. "Say the widening buys two years. Say that's real. What happens in year three?"

"Nobody in any of these comments says," Alexander admitted. "That's the part I can't get past. I'm going to stand up there and tell them the lanes will fill, because the evidence says they will. But I can't stand up there and tell Teo's dad to keep losing forty minutes, or your mom to risk a client, so that a number behaves." He underlined bus frequency twice. "Maybe the honest speech is that the widening can't be the whole answer and we have to say what the other half is."

Ms. Chen came through on her way to the reference desk, paused, and read his two headings upside down with the neutrality of someone grading on process. "Two minutes," she reminded him. "Rehearse it out loud at least once."

After she'd gone, Kaia read his list, crossed out one line, added another in her slanted hand, and pushed it back. "Start with my mom," she said. "Start there, then give them the word."

Alexander stood, faced the empty chairs, and began.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
Edgar's kitchen smelled of burnt toast and dish soap, and on the table between them lay a folded newspaper, one article circled in pencil. Sarah had promised herself she would read it aloud before the toast smell faded, which was a way of giving the task a deadline nobody had set.

"Okay," she said. "Segundo párrafo."

She had been studying Spanish for three months, mostly through an app on the bus, and this was the first real thing she had tried to read. Edgar's mother took the paper, El Diario, from the bodega on the corner, and Edgar had offered it with the shrug of someone doing her a favor he did not understand. He sat across from her now, eating a second, unburnt slice of toast, his chemistry notebook open beside him. He was supposed to be reviewing for a test on polymers, and every few minutes he wrote the word monomer and drew a little circle with two arms reaching out of it.

Sarah worked through the second paragraph slowly, sounding out words, and then stopped. "Según la portavoz de la empresa, el vertido no representa ningún riesgo." She looked up. "According to the spokesperson of the company, the spill does not represent any risk."

"So the spill is safe," Edgar said.

"No." She put her finger on the word. "That's not what it says. It says según. It means 'according to.' The paper isn't saying the spill is safe. The paper is saying the company's spokesperson said the spill is safe."

Edgar chewed on that along with his toast. "Isn't that the same thing?"

"It's the opposite thing." She read the rest of the paragraph again and found two more claims, one introduced by según and one flat, bare statement about how many liters had spilled. The liters were the paper's own fact. The safety was somebody's sentence that the paper was carrying, like a package with a return address on it. "The reporters use según to show where a claim comes from. It tells you the statement is from a source, not from them."

"So when you summarize it, what do you say?"

That was the actual assignment, and it was due Monday. Mr. Lin had assigned each student a short article in a new language and three minutes at the front of the room: read a passage, summarize it aloud, in English, saying what the article claimed and how confident you were that the claim was true. Sarah had drawn Spanish. She had been relieved until she opened the paper and found the article about the spill, which was two towns over, upstream of a reservoir.

"Here's my problem," she said. "If I say 'the spill doesn't pose any risk,' I'm lying, because that's not established, that's a quote. If I say 'the company says the spill doesn't pose any risk,' I'm accurate, but it sounds like I'm dunking on the company, and I don't actually know they're wrong. Maybe it is safe. I have no idea how many liters of what, in what water."

"So give both," Edgar said, and wrote monomer again, a longer chain this time, circles holding hands. "Like, the fact is a fact and the claim is a claim. That's all Mr. Lin wants, right?"

"Mr. Lin wants us to be able to read something and say what it says. He said that on day one. He said the summary has to be pithy, his word, pithy, three minutes." She tried it out. "A pipeline spilled an estimated eight thousand liters of wastewater into Cedar Creek on Tuesday. According to the company, the spill poses no risk to the reservoir. According to a state environmental official, testing won't be complete until Friday."

Edgar's mother came in for coffee, took the paper, read the headline, clicked her tongue, and left again without comment, which Sarah understood to be its own summary.

She tried it again, and it came out smoother, and then she saw the hole in it. Both claims were sourced, both were según, and she was setting them side by side as if they carried equal weight, when one came from the party responsible for the spill and one came from someone whose job was testing. The paper hadn't ranked them. It had just attributed both, cleanly, and let the verbs do the quiet work. To summarize honestly she had to do what the paper did, attribute everything, and then add one sentence of her own that historicized it, placing each speaker in the situation that shaped their saying. But she didn't know enough to place them. She knew only who spoke, not why.

"I'll say who said what," she told Edgar. "And then I'll say I don't know which one is right yet, and why I don't. That's the honest version."

"That's going to sound so boring."

"It's going to sound like Monday." She folded the paper on its crease and put it in her bag, next to her Spanish flashcards and the water bottle she kept forgetting to fill.

Edgar closed his notebook, chains of little circles marching across the last page, and slid it toward her. "Quiz me on this instead," he said. "If I fail polymers, my mom's version of según is going to be 'according to your teacher.'"

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The coefficients in a balanced chemical equation give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of hot glue and floor wax, and the judges would begin their rounds in fifty minutes. Anais stood beside her poster, which described the reaction of baking soda with vinegar, and watched Talia across the aisle arranging and rearranging the same three sheets of paper as though a different order might change what was printed on them.

"Everything okay?" Anais asked, crossing over.

Talia flattened a corner with her palm. "My numbers are stupid. I predicted twelve grams of sodium acetate from what I used, and when I weighed what I actually got, it was less than nine. So either my scale is broken or the reaction didn't finish." Her voice had the flatness of someone who had already decided which answer she preferred.

Anais read the poster top to bottom. Talia had written her equation, balanced it, and then underneath it, in confident marker, she had taken her grams of baking soda and multiplied by the ratio of the coefficients in the equation, as if the numbers written before each formula were a recipe measured in grams. The product of that arithmetic hung there, grand and wrong. Anais felt something atavistic stir in her, the old pleasure of spotting an error on someone else's page, the kind she used to chase in middle school before she learned how small it made her feel.

"Where'd you get that step?" she asked, keeping her voice neutral.

"The coefficients. One to one to one to one. It's all ones, so I just carried the grams straight across." Talia tapped the balanced equation. "That's legal, right?"

Anais did not answer right away, because she was not sure. She herself had spent two evenings with her calculator and a periodic table, dividing grams by molar masses, converting everything into moles before she let the coefficients touch it, and she had begun to suspect that the distinction mattered more than she could yet say. "I think the coefficients are a ratio of moles, not masses," she said slowly. "Not grams. Moles. Like, the equation is counting particles, not weighing them." She heard how tentative it sounded, and she let it sound that way, because it was.

Talia stared at her own poster. "So I did the whole thing in the wrong units."

"Try it in moles. Your molar masses are on the back there." Anais pulled a pencil from behind Talia's pencil cup without asking, an old habit between them, and Talia laughed once, a short cracked sound, and began dividing.

The gymnasium doors opened and Ms. Lindqvist came through with a clipboard and two other judges, moving down the far row first, which gave Talia maybe twenty minutes. Anais stood beside her while she worked, checking each division, watching the predicted number shrink and then shrink again until it settled just under nine grams, close enough to the true weight on the balance that Talia put her hand over her mouth. "It was never the reaction," she said. "It was me." She said it as though confessing to something larger than arithmetic, and in a way she was; the error had let her believe for two days that her experiment had failed when only her model of it had.

"You have to redo the whole results section," Anais said.

"In twenty minutes."

"So start tearing."

They tore. Talia sliced the old sheet off the poster with a scissors from the supply table while Anais rewrote the calculation in her neatest hand, converting grams to moles first, letting the coefficients do their work on the moles only, then converting back to grams at the end. When Anais reached the final line she paused, because she wanted to write a sentence explaining the principle, making it explicit for the judges, and Talia shook her head. "If they ask, I'll say it myself. It has to come out of my mouth or it isn't mine." Anais surrendered the marker. That was the cost of the morning, she understood: she had found the error, but the finding belonged now to Talia, who would carry it in her own voice, and Anais would stand one aisle over with her own tidy poster and no part of it.

The judges reached their row with six minutes to spare. Ms. Lindqvist read the new results sheet, tilted her head at the balanced equation, and asked Talia why she had converted to moles before applying the coefficients. Talia said, "Because the coefficients give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses," and then, glancing once at Anais, she added nothing more, and Ms. Lindqvist wrote something on her clipboard that neither of them could see.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Robert Millikan measured the charge of the electron by using the electric field between two horizontal charged plates to hold tiny charged oil drops still against gravity.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and machine oil, and Julia had claimed the workbench closest to the window because its light fell clean across her notebook. She had failed the physics quiz on Tuesday. Not barely failed, failed in a way that Mr. Abdi, her neighbour, had described as "a fork in the road" when she dragged her practice setup over to his side of the fence. He had lent her two square metal plates, a variable power supply with a frayed cord, and a plastic tackle box of clips and wires, then gone inside to make tea and left her alone with the whole question.

The question was this: find the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates. On paper it was one line, voltage divided by separation. On the bench it was a mess of clips and doubt. Sabine sat on an overturned bucket, holding the multimeter, reading numbers aloud in a flat voice that Julia found both steadying and faintly accusatory. "Twelve point one volts," Sabine said. "Twelve point oh eight. Twelve point one again." Julia adjusted the gap between the plates, five centimetres by her ruler, and wrote the numbers in a column, then divided, then crossed it out and did it again because the second decimal kept moving.

"I don't get what I'm even computing," Julia said. "It's a number. It's volts over centimetres. So what?" A pass on Monday's retest would enfranchise her into the second-year stream, the one with the real labs, the one that colleges wanted to see, and she could feel the weight of that whenever she let herself think about it, which was why she mostly didn't. Sabine, whose ambitions ran toward literature and who viewed physics with a mild, jaundiced skepticism, shrugged. "So the field is pushing something. That's what fields do, right? They push."

Julia had propped the plates vertical at first, because that was how the textbook drew them, and she had balanced a sliver of aluminium foil between them and watched it swing sideways and stick. It was Jordan, texting from the science museum across town, who changed the arrangement. He had gone with his little brother on Saturday and sent her a photo of a replica of some old apparatus, all brass and glass, with a caption: "is this the thing from ur unit?" The photo showed two horizontal plates, one above the other, with a small chamber between them. Julia stared at it for a long time, thumb over the screen, before she understood what she was looking at. The plates were horizontal. The field between them pointed up or down. Against gravity.

"Wait," she said out loud, and tipped her whole rig sideways, plates first, so that one hung above the other. Sabine watched with the expression of someone seeing a friend rearrange furniture in a burning house. Julia read the placard text Jordan typed out next, slowly, because her signal was bad in the garage: Robert Millikan measured the charge of the electron with this. He used the electric field between two horizontal charged plates to hold tiny charged oil drops still against gravity. She read it twice. "Oil drops," she said. "He held them still. That was the whole trick. Gravity pulls down, the field pushes up, and if the drop just hangs there, you can work out its charge."

"So the number in your notebook," Sabine said, "that volts-over-centimetres thing, that's the push." Julia said yes, and meant it, and also felt the limits of the yes. She knew the field was uniform between the plates in the ideal case, and she knew her plates were not ideal, were scuffed and slightly crooked, and that the foil was not a charged oil drop but a bent scrap she had torn from a gum wrapper. Somewhere between the clean line on the quiz and the humming bench in the garage there was a gap she could not yet close, and she was honest enough with herself to sit in that gap rather than pretend it wasn't there. The genealogy of what she was doing ran from Coulomb through Millikan to a Tuesday morning quiz, and she liked knowing she was holding the recent end of a very old rope, even if her grip was unsure.

She charged the foil by rubbing it on her sleeve, which felt absurd, and dropped it through a hole Mr. Abdi had drilled in the top plate years ago for reasons he had never explained. The first time, the foil fell straight through. The second time she raised the voltage and it shot upward and stuck to the plate. The third time, she nudged the dial with the patience of someone defusing something, and the foil entered the space between the plates and stopped. It hung there. Not falling, not sticking. Suspended, trembling a little in whatever small air moved through the garage, held up by nothing she could see, by a field she had computed in a column of crossed-out numbers.

"Julia," Sabine said, very quietly, as if the foil might be startled. "It's still." Julia reached for her notebook to calculate the charge on the wrapper scrap, following Millikan's logic the way you follow footprints, and it was then that she saw the black alligator clip lying on the concrete under the bench, where it had fallen, and traced its wire back to the supply, and realized the plug had been loose for who knew how long. She looked up. The foil was still floating, serene, unassisted, above the plates.

"You've got to be kidding me," she said, and the foil drifted down and landed softly on the lower plate, like it had only been waiting for her to notice.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: By the JavaBeans naming convention, a getter for a field named 'score' is called getScore(), and a getter for a boolean field is usually named with 'is', like isActive().
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm monitors and the janitor's lemon cleaner, and Benjamin had been staring at the same forty lines of Karan's code for eleven minutes. Their project was due Friday. Karan had written the Player class over the weekend while Benjamin was at his grandmother's, and now nothing matched. The field was called score, fine, but the method that returned it was called fetchTheScore, and the one for the boolean field active was called isPlayerCurrentlyOn, which was not the same thing at all.

"You named it fetchTheScore," Benjamin said, spinning his chair around. "Like it's a dog."

"Retrieval is retrieval," Karan said, ebullient, entirely unbothered, chewing a pen cap. "It's expressive."

"It's a heist. The score is being stolen."

Jayden leaned over from the next terminal, where he was supposed to be writing the test class and was instead reading about drone racing. "What's wrong with it? It compiles."

That was the problem, Benjamin thought, or rather said, because saying it out loud made it feel more like a problem and less like a mood. It compiled. Every method did what it claimed. But the test file Mr. Rao had given them expected certain names, and more than that, anyone reading the code would expect certain names, the way you expect a door handle at hand height. Benjamin had learned the convention somewhere, maybe half-asleep during a video, maybe from Jayden's notes, and it had stuck: a getter for a field named score is called getScore(), and a getter for a boolean field usually starts with is, like isActive.

"We should just rename everything," he said. "Field's score, so the getter is getScore. Boolean's active, so it's isActive. That's the JavaBeans convention."

Karan removed the pen cap and pointed it at him. "Beans."

"Convention. It's just what people do."

"People also used to think the sun went around the earth, conventionally." But Karan was already pulling the file toward himself, muttering, resizing the window with the violence of a man being asked to cauterize his own prose. Benjamin felt a small pang of complicity in the renaming, as though they were erasing Karan's authorship together, one find-and-replace at a time, and said so. Karan said that was the most dramatic thing anyone had ever said about a method name, and renamed fetchTheScore anyway.

Then they hit the part that mattered. The test class, the one Mr. Rao would actually run, called getScore() on a Player object and compared it to a number, and called isActive() and checked whether the player was still in the game. Jayden finally wrote the real test: make a player, set the score to ten, add five, assert that getScore() returned fifteen, then set active to false and assert that isActive() returned false. It failed twice before it passed, once because Karan had left a stray print statement that turned fifteen into "15 coins!!!", and once because Benjamin, in a fit of tidiness, had made the score field public and forgotten the getter entirely, which Jayden found so funny he screenshotted it.

Mr. Rao drifted over during the third run, hands behind his back, reading the screen without touching anything. "Whose naming?"

"His," they said together, and then, "Mine," also together, which Mr. Rao appeared to find sufficient. He watched the green checkmark appear on the passing test, nodded once, and drifted toward the door where two students were arguing about semicolons with rising voices.

"So the convention," Karan said, saving the file, "is it in the textbook, or is it just vibes that everyone agreed to?"

Benjamin opened his mouth to say he was pretty sure, then closed it, because he genuinely didn't know whether it was written down somewhere official or just the accumulated habit of a few million people deciding, separately, that fetchTheScore was a crime. "Both, maybe," he said. "I'd have to look it up."

"Look it up while I get snacks," Karan said, standing. "The beans deserve justice." He pointed at the screen on his way out, at the little green bar. "Leave that running. I want to see it again when I'm back."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, a ball dropped from a table and a ball launched horizontally from the same height hit a level floor at the same time.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and vinegar from the volcano exhibit two tables over, which had gone off early and unsupervised. Benjamin stood behind his tri-fold board, PROJECTILE MOTION IN TWO INDEPENDENT DIMENSIONS, and watched the judges make their slow way down the aisle like weather.

"You rehearsed the part where you look casual?" Camilo asked. He was there for moral support and, reportedly, free pizza in the lounge, though the lounge had run out of pizza at ten.

"I rehearsed dropping things off tables," Benjamin said. "The casual part ossified around hour three."

He had a ramp, a steel ball, a table borrowed from the cafeteria, and a second steel ball he intended to simply release from the same height. The math on his board showed the two motions separated: the horizontal velocity doing its steady work in one column, gravity doing its work in another, neither one consulting the other. That was the whole idea. Two columns. He had written and rewritten the final sentence until it stopped sounding grandiose and started sounding like something he could defend.

Adelyn arrived with her clipboard, because she had appointed herself timekeeper, and because she had bet Camilo five dollars on the outcome. Camilo had taken the dropped ball. "It starts falling immediately," he said. "The other one is busy going sideways. Sideways takes energy away."

"That's not a sentence that means anything," Adelyn said.

"It means five dollars."

Ms. Somsak, who taught physics two doors down from the study hall where Benjamin had spent a month not understanding any of this, paused at the table. She looked at the board, then at the table, then at the line of tape on the floor where the launched ball was supposed to land. "You're going to do it live," she said. Not a question.

"Six times," Benjamin said. "Averaged by ear."

"By ear," she repeated, and moved on, though he noticed she didn't go far.

The problem had started as a want, honestly, and a small one. He had wanted to stop guessing. Every problem set in the unit had felt like a coin flip dressed up in algebra, and he'd compensated with confidence, which is what a person does instead of understanding. Then one night, at his grandmother's kitchen table, he'd flicked a bottle cap off the edge while doing the dishes and noticed he could not say, before it hit, whether it had left his hand a tenth of a second before or after an identical cap he'd simply tipped over the edge. He'd stood there with wet hands for a while. The two columns had begun there, at the sink.

"Judges at two tables," Adelyn reported. "Also a man with a lanyard who might be a judge or might be lost."

Benjamin set both balls on the table edge. "One drops straight," he said. "One leaves horizontally. Same height. Level floor. We listen for the sounds."

"One sound or two?" Camilo asked, taking out his phone anyway, as if the phone would arbitrate.

"If I've done this right," Benjamin said, "you won't be able to tell them apart."

The first judge arrived mid-setup, a woman with a pen behind her ear like a carpenter's pencil. She read the board while Benjamin held both balls, one in each hand, over the same line of tape. He let one fall and flicked the other along the ramp, and the launched ball crossed the room in its flat, businesslike arc while the dropped ball thumped the shadow beneath it. Two sounds arrived so close together that Camilo, who had his phone raised to record the gap for posterity and for five dollars, lowered it again.

"Again," Adelyn said.

He did it again. The dropped ball struck; the launched ball struck; the interval between them was smaller than the interval between the syllables of "again." On the fourth run they landed so nearly together that Camilo said, with dignity, "I heard a slight preference for mine."

"You heard the echo," Adelyn said. She wrote something on her clipboard, and did not hand over five dollars.

The judge with the pen asked him what would happen if he launched the ball faster. Benjamin said the time to the floor would not change; it would just land farther away, and that this was the part he'd refused to believe for three weeks, which was why the exhibit existed. She asked what he'd do differently. He said he'd like a second ramp at a different speed, to show the landing point moving while the landing time stayed put, and admitted he hadn't built it yet.

The second judge joined the first. Ms. Somsak drifted back with a coffee she had clearly carried halfway across the gymnasium for this purpose. Camilo was negotiating with Adelyn over whether "basically simultaneous" constituted a tie.

"I'll build the second ramp tonight," Benjamin said to the judges. "The floor here is level. I checked with a marble."

The woman with the pen wrote something down. From two tables over came another small volcanic report, and the lost man with the lanyard began applauding, alone, at nothing.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
story:
The ground was soft from three days of rain, and Julia's heels sank in as the rabbi finished speaking. Her grandmother's coffin rested on straps beside the grave, and when the shovel came around, Julia took it. Her father had told her it was customary for the family to put the first earth on the coffin, and she did it, one shovelful, then another, because someone had to and because she wanted to be the one. The dirt hit the wood with a sound she knew she would remember.

Aila stood at the back of the crowd with Katia. They had driven an hour on a school morning, and they waited until the family began walking back toward the cars before they came forward. Aila hugged Julia quickly, the way you hug someone when you are not sure hugging is allowed. "We have to go back by fifth period," Katia said, and then looked sorry she had said it.

"There's a thing after," Julia said. "At my grandmother's apartment. My dad wants people to come."

Aila glanced at Katia. "Is that the thing where you sit for a week? My cousin did it when my uncle died." She paused, working it out. "They call it shiva. It means seven."

Julia nodded. She had heard the word that morning from her father, in the car, but she had not caught what it meant until now. Seven days, starting after the burial. It was already starting, she realized; the clock on it had begun the moment the last of the dirt went in.

The apartment smelled like the coffee people had brought and like the tuna sandwiches the neighbor had made, because you were not supposed to cook for yourself, someone had said, and Julia had filed that away without asking who had decided. People kept saying "may her memory be a blessing," and Julia said it back, and then stopped saying it because she was saying it to people who had come to comfort her, and it felt backwards. In the living room, her grandmother's bookshelf still held the paperbacks with cracked spines. There was a philosophy anthology Julia had flipped through once, the summer she was fifteen, and she remembered her grandmother tapping a page and saying, "Existentialism. The idea that you make your own meaning, bubbe. It's not for the faint of heart." Julia had said something dismissive at the time. She took the book down now and did not open it.

She found herself thinking that her grandmother had liked rules the way some people like fences, not to be confined but to know where the edges were. Seven days of sitting. A week in which the calendar itself codified grief, so that no one had to guess how long to be sad or when to stop. Julia had spent the last six months assuming grief was the opposite, something formless that you were supposed to figure out alone. At school, in the college essay drafts Ms. Gallagher had returned in March, Julia had written that she wanted a life with no predetermined shapes, and Ms. Gallagher had written in the margin, "Be careful what you wish for." She understood the note differently now.

Her father was sanguine in a way that unsettled her, greeting relatives, pouring seltzer, telling the story of the time his mother had returned a rented car spotless and complained about the smell of the cleaner. He was not faking it, she decided. He was seven days into a structure that held him up, and he did not have to think about what came next because what came next was already laid out. Julia had refused to take the chair her aunt offered her at first, standing by the window, keeping her options open, and around four o'clock she changed her mind and sat down in it. The chair was lower than the others, she noticed, and when she asked her aunt why, her aunt said, "You're the mourner. You're supposed to be comfortable." Julia could not tell whether that was true or whether her aunt was inventing it, and she let the question go.

Aila and Katia came back the next evening with a plastic container of pasta from Katia's mother. They stood in the doorway holding it until Julia waved them in. "I didn't know if you'd be sick of food," Aila said. "There's so much food."

"There's always going to be this much food," Julia said. "I checked the fridge. There are nine lasagnas."

"Ten," Katia said, setting hers down on the counter next to a tin of cookies. "You're welcome."

Julia pulled them toward the living room, past the philosophy book still lying face-down on the arm of the chair, and pointed at the low seat she had claimed. "That one's mine," she said. "For six more days."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: The Surrealist André Breton described Kahlo's art as "a ribbon around a bomb," though Kahlo herself later rejected the Surrealist label.
story:
Emilie had taped a print of Frida Kahlo's "The Two Fridas" above her desk with washi tape shaped like tiny cacti, which she considered both decoration and an argument. Jayda sat cross-legged on the bed with her laptop open, eating dry cereal out of the box like a woman with no obligations, which was exactly what she was supposed to be pretending to be.

"We need an actual thesis," Emilie said. "Not 'the colours are sad because she was sad.' Ms. Mercado circled that exact sentence on my last paper and wrote, 'Feelings are not evidence.'"

"Ms. Mercado circled something on mine too," Jayda said, peering into the box. "It just said 'No.' She's so economical. It's almost elegant."

Emilie turned back to the painting. The duplicated woman on the left, in the white European dress with the lace bleeding out onto her skirt. The woman on the right, in the Tehuana dress, holding the tiny portrait of the man connecting them by that absurd exposed vein. Her assignment sheet said formal analysis: colour, composition, symbolism, in that order, and she had a page of notes that read like a hostage negotiation between three different versions of herself.

"Okay, so the composition first," she said. "Two figures, symmetrical, joined at the hands and the heart. The sky behind them is stormy but almost empty, so your eye has nowhere to go except into the bodies. That's deliberate. That's not sad, that's engineering."

"Write that down, that's actually good," Jayda said, mouth full. "You should also mention the blood, probably. There's a lot of blood for a formal analysis. Unless blood doesn't count as form."

"Everything counts as form if you're brave about it."

Rayne, who was on Emilie's phone in the group chat from across town, disagreed. Emilie read the message aloud: "Rayne says Kahlo's obviously a Surrealist, dream logic, double self, so just frame the whole paper around Surrealism and be done."

Jayda made a small scornful noise, phlegmatic except for the eyebrows, which were doing all the disagreeing her voice refused to. "Rayne says that because Rayne read one paragraph on a museum website in eleventh grade and has been coasting on it ever since."

"Rayne reads more than both of us," Emilie said, but she typed anyway, and the argument migrated to the phone while she was also supposed to be writing, which was how she worked best, apparently, in a state of low-grade chaos. Then she stopped typing, because something was nagging at her.

She remembered sitting in Ms. Mercado's classroom in the spring, the afternoon light doing that thing where it turned the whiteboard green and nobody could read it anyway. Ms. Mercado had said a quote and refused to say who said it, made them sit with it, which at the time had felt like a cruel yoga pose. A ribbon around a bomb. Emilie had written it in the margin of her notebook and then, in a fit of tidiness that clearly stemmed from some other Emilie, some more organized Emilie she was always failing to become, circled it.

"Wait," she said, and dug through her backpack, past a fossilized granola bar, to the notebook. "Here. Somebody called her work 'a ribbon around a bomb.'"

"Who?"

"That's the thing, I didn't write it down, I was too busy being annoyed at the exercise." She took the laptop from Jayda, less politely than intended, and searched. It took three tries and one deeply unhelpful website about ribbon crafts before she found it: André Breton, the Surrealist, the one who'd basically run Surrealism like a club with a bouncer.

"Okay so listen," Emilie said. "Breton described her art as 'a ribbon around a bomb.'" She said it slowly, the way you handle something that might be load-bearing. "But get this. Kahlo herself later rejected the Surrealist label."

Jayda set down the cereal box, which was the cereal box equivalent of standing up. "Rejected it? Rayne is going to be devastated. Rayne has called her a Surrealist in at least four essays."

The phone buzzed. Rayne: "Are you ignoring me because you know I'm right?"

Emilie typed: "You're wrong, actually. She rejected the label. Breton called her work 'a ribbon around a bomb' and she said no thanks to the whole Surrealist thing."

A long pause, then: "??? she's OBVIOUSLY a surrealist."

"Obviously," Jayda said over Emilie's shoulder, "means you haven't checked."

But Emilie was staring at the print again, and the problem had gotten bigger, which was, she suspected, what Ms. Mercado meant by thinking. Because Rayne wasn't entirely wrong. The doubled self, the exposed heart, the vein like a garden hose of the psyche, that was dream logic, that did instantiate the Surrealist playbook. And yet Kahlo had said no to it, insisted she painted her own reality, not her dreams, and Emilie could see the difference now, in the composition itself. A dream would dissolve the two women into each other. This painting kept them stubbornly separate, joined only by that one artery, each Frida fully rendered, fully awake. It was a wedding portrait of a divorce. It was too specific to be a dream.

"So what's the thesis?" Jayda said. "You have that face. The face you get when you're about to make the paper harder on purpose."

"The thesis is that it uses Surrealist strategies and refuses the Surrealist claim," Emilie said, typing. "Or, no. The thesis is that the disagreement is the point. The bomb and the ribbon are arguing with each other, and Breton only saw the ribbon, and Kahlo only claimed the bomb, and the painting is both of them being wrong in a productive way. Formal analysis section: the symmetry, the empty sky, the blood as line and as symbol at the same time."

"That's good," Jayda admitted. "It's annoying how good it is. I was going to write about the monkeys."

"Rayne's going to say we ganged up on her."

The phone buzzed. Rayne: "Fine. FINE. But if you two are turning this into some big synthesis thing I want credit for the wrong position. Every good argument needs someone to be wrong first."

Emilie laughed and pulled the laptop closer, and above her the two Fridas held hands in the storm, one heart cut and one heart whole, connected by the only vein in the room that mattered.

"Okay," she said. "Paragraph one. Colour."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word diploma comes from a Greek word meaning "paper folded double," from the earlier practice of folding official documents.
story:
Addison arrived at Il Forno twenty minutes early, which gave her time to rearrange the napkin three times and to decide that the napkin looked better the first way. Her mother had booked the long table by the window for the whole family, but only half of them had come, and the empty chairs at the far end had a way of drawing the eye. She was seventeen as of March, and graduated as of eleven o'clock that morning, and somewhere between those two facts her stomach had knotted itself into something she could not name.

Arya slid into the seat across from her, still in her gown, which she had rolled at the waist and tied with the cord of her hood like a belt. "I have worn this thing for six hours," Arya said, "and I refuse to take it off until someone makes me." Her father, following behind with a balloon that said CONGRATULATIONS in letters designed by someone who had never met a teenager, asked for a table for six, then a table for five, then gave up and let the hostess sort it out.

"Look at this," Addison said. She had the diploma folder in front of her on the tablecloth, a leatherette case with the school's crest stamped in gold that had already begun to flake at one corner. She opened it flat, and there lay the certificate, a single unfolded sheet, her name in script that a machine had chosen, the ink so fresh she suspected it of drying during the ceremony itself. "Four years. Twelve hundred dollars in fund-raising chocolate. One unfolded piece of paper."

Jai dropped into the chair beside Arya and leaned over the folder. "At my cousin's graduation, they handed out empty folders," he said. "The diplomas came in the mail in July, because they said people lose them at the ceremony. Can you imagine? You walk the stage for a folder with nothing inside it."

Addison ran her thumb along the creaseless edge of the sheet. "You know what the word actually is?" she said, and then stopped, because she was not sure she did. She had read it somewhere in April, in the waiting room of the dentist, in a magazine article about the history of letters, and she had carried it around since without checking it against anything. "Diploma. It comes from a Greek word meaning paper folded double. That's where the whole word starts. From the practice back then of folding official documents."

Arya picked up her own diploma folder and opened it, squinting at the flat page. "So the folder is the honest part," she said, "and the paper is a liar."

"Double," Jai said, holding up two fingers like he was testing the arithmetic. "This is one. Someone at the factory owes us a fold."

The waitress came, a woman with a pen behind each ear, and took a drink order complicated by Addison's grandmother, who wanted to know whether the espresso was real espresso or, and here she lowered her voice as though confessing to a scheme, airport espresso. Addison ordered the lemon chicken she had been thinking about since the English exam, and when the menus were collected she found that the conversation had moved on without her, to Ms. Navarro, who was at another table across the room with a party of her own.

Ms. Navarro had taught Addison's government class, the one where they had argued about populists and technocrats for a full week in February, and Addison had written her final essay on the difference between a politician who listened to people and one who only imitated listening, a distinction she had believed in firmly for exactly four days. She caught Ms. Navarro's eye across the room and raised a hand, and Ms. Navarro raised her water glass, and that was the whole exchange, and it felt like both enough and not nearly.

"She gave me a B plus," Addison said, mostly to the table.

"On what?"

"The essay. I thought it was the best thing I wrote all year. I expatiated for two pages on leadership." She heard the word come out of her mouth and heard, at the same time, how it must sound, and Arya laughed so hard the balloon string swung.

"Two pages," Jai said. "She stopped you at two pages. That's the most canny thing a teacher ever did to a person who talks like that."

The food came, and the noise around the table rearranged itself, as it does when plates arrive, into a hundred small negotiations over bread and parmesan and whose iced tea was whose. Addison ate her chicken slowly. She was thinking about the unfolded paper and the B plus and the way Ms. Navarro had raised her glass, and she was trying to decide whether she actually believed the thing about the Greek, whether a word could carry its old meaning inside it like a folded page, or whether that was just something a magazine had told her once and she had adopted because it sounded true. She had spent four years collecting facts like that, at the dentist, in class, from Jai's cousins, and she could not always remember which ones she had verified and which ones she had simply liked.

In September she would be two hundred miles east, in a dormitory whose roommate she had spoken to twice, both times awkwardly, once about a mini fridge. Arya would be forty minutes from here, at the state school, and Jai was taking a year to work at his uncle's shop and think, which his father called drifting and Jai called research. All three of them had said, at some point during senior year, that nothing would change, and all three of them had said it with the particular insistence of people who suspected otherwise. Addison looked down the long table, past her grandmother breaking bread, past the empty chairs, and thought that the folder was the part you kept and the paper was the part that said what happened, and that the two things were not the same, and that she had no idea which one she was supposed to be holding onto.

Arya's phone buzzed, and Arya read something on it, and did not say what it was, and put it face down next to the bread basket. Addison watched her do it and did not ask. Tomorrow there would be a time to ask. There would be a whole summer of times to ask, most of which they would not use.

"So," Jai said, lifting his glass of iced tea as though it were champagne, "to the folded paper." He tapped the diploma folder with one finger. "Folded double, by law, by tradition, and by the Greeks."

"To the Greeks," Arya said, raising hers.

Addison raised her water glass last. Then she picked up the diploma, folded it once, crisply, down the middle, and set it back in the folder the way it had apparently been meant to lie. Her mother, three seats down, said, "You'll crease it, honey," and Addison said, "That's the point."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: A primary source was produced at the time being studied, such as a letter or diary, while a secondary source, such as a textbook, interprets the past later using primary sources.
story:
The box had been under the sideboard at his grandmother's house for as long as Seth could remember, and at every gathering someone threatened to open it and nobody did. This year, the year Seth turned seventeen, his grandmother set it on the kitchen table between the potato salad and the platter of ham and said, "Somebody should go through these before I'm not around to say who anybody is." Then she went back to basting, and the box sat there like a dare.

Seth's cousin's boyfriend, a college sophomore everyone called Byron whether he liked it or not, pulled the lid off first. Inside were letters, dozens of them, still in their envelopes, tied with shoelace. The return address said a name Seth half recognized from overheard arguments: his great-uncle, the one who had either walked out of the family business or been pushed out of it, depending on which aunt you asked. Seth had a reason to care. He'd written his history paper last spring on the family's old hardware store and had gotten a B minus because, as Mr. Martínez put it in red ink, he'd relied on "one textbook account of downtown decline" and never asked what the people who lived it had to say. The paper still itched at him.

"These are primary sources," Byron said, turning an envelope over. "Produced right when it happened. A letter like this, or a diary. Not like your textbook, which interprets the whole thing later, using these." He said it casually, the way he said most things, as though he were reading off a receipt, and went back to his phone. Seth had heard the terms in Mr. Martínez's class in March and had let them slide past him like weather. Now he was holding one.

He read the first letter standing up, a corner of napkin under his elbow to keep the tablecloth clean. The great-uncle wrote to his brother in a cramped, urgent hand about money, about a loan the brother had promised and then, apparently, withdrawn. The second letter was angrier. The third, from the brother back, was bombastic in a way that made Seth wince, full of phrases like "the honor of this family" and "posterity will judge," and it prognosticated ruin for everyone if the loan went through, which Seth noted had a certain symmetry with the actual ruin that came later, though not for the reason given.

The argument started before dessert. One aunt held that the great-uncle had abandoned the store out of pride; an uncle held that the brother had frozen him out over a woman nobody would name. Both of them leaned on the letters now, over Seth's shoulder, each finding the sentence that proved her case. "Read that part again," the uncle said, tapping a line about trust. "He's apologizing," the aunt said, tapping the same line, "that's a confession."

Seth wanted to settle it, and he understood, in a way he couldn't have articulated in March, that he wanted it too much. The letters were partial. They were produced at the time, by people with reasons to shade things, and there were gaps you could fall into. He thought of the textbook again, the smooth paragraph about the decline of downtown, and how it must have been built out of exactly this kind of paper, sifted and smoothed until it sounded like nobody had ever written it. Somewhere between the letter and the textbook, the argument had been laundered out. He didn't know yet whether that was a loss or a mercy.

"Ask her," Byron said, nodding toward the grandmother, who was carrying out the cake. Seth hesitated. She was the last one who'd been in the room, so to speak, and whatever she said would become, in his mind, the secondary source, the later interpretation, and he'd have to weigh it against the envelopes without knowing how much of her account had itself been assembled from other people's versions.

He asked. She set the cake down, looked at the letters for a long moment, and said, "That shoelace was mine. I tied it when I was nine because they were all over the floor and I was tired of them." Then she cut the cake.

Later, on the porch with the box resealed and the shoelace retied, Seth sat with Stephan, a classmate who'd come by for the leftovers. Stephan read two of the letters under the porch light and said, "So who was right, the aunt or the uncle?" Seth said he didn't know, that the letters disagreed with each other, and that he suspected the question itself had changed shape somewhere between 1962 and this afternoon. Stephan said, "That's not an answer." Seth took the letters back, squared the envelopes against his knee, and said, "It's the one the sources give." Down the hall, the screen door clapped shut behind the last of the guests.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Schenck v. United States (1919), Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.
story:
I have never lost an argument in my life, which is exactly why Ms. Oliveira assigned me both sides of the mock court. That is her version of a joke. She handed me the folder at the end of fifth period, when the hallway smelled like floor wax and someone's microwaved nachos, and said, "Mr. Silverman for the petitioner, Mr. Silverman for the respondent," which was not even my name, but I took the folder anyway because the alternative was the lost-and-found bin of debate topics nobody wanted.

The case was about a student suspended for a poster, and the whole thing supposedly turned on the First Amendment. Fine. I had done free speech before. I figured I'd spend one evening on it and spend the rest of the week teaching Dave to stop opening his arguments with "basically."

Dave did not need my help, which was the first sign the week was going badly. We set up in the library after school, at the table by the window where the radiators clank like a small trapped animal, and he flipped through my folder while I pretended to outline. "You've got Holmes in here," he said. "The fire thing."

"Obviously," I said, though I had not read that far.

"'The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic,'" he read out loud, doing a voice like a ship captain. "That's Schenck, 1919. You're quoting it for the school, right? Speech that causes panic isn't protected."

"For the school, obviously," I said again, and wrote it down, and that is when Anton slid into the seat across from us with his laconic little grin, the one he deploys when he knows something you don't, which is more often than I like to admit.

"Read him the whole case," Anton said.

"I know the whole case," I said, which was a lie, and Dave, traitor that he is, started reading anyway. Schenck had been convicted for circulating pamphlets against the draft. Holmes wrote the opinion upholding the conviction. The fire line came from the man locking the door, not opening it.

"Wait," I said. The radiator clanked twice, as if it agreed. "The most famous pro-speech quote in America is from the guy saying speech isn't protected?"

"Falsely shouting fire," Anton corrected, holding up one finger, "in a theatre, causing a panic. Nineteen nineteen. Holmes. That's the whole sentence, and that's all of it. People exhume that line every time they want to win an argument, and half of them don't know who they're digging up."

This was infuriating, partly because he was right and partly because he said "exhume" the way other people say "hey." I took my folder back from Dave and started over from page one, which I should have done the first time, but in my defense, I was very busy being confident.

Here is the thing about arguing both sides that nobody warns you about. You start noticing that each side has a good argument and also a lazy one. The school's lazy argument was the fire quote, waved around like a cross at a vampire. The student's lazy argument was "First Amendment," said in a tone that suggested the words were magic. The good arguments were harder. The poster disrupted a math class, or it didn't. The school punished a viewpoint, or it punished a disruption. My outline began to look like a rationalism problem, pure logic with no people in it, and I kept having to shove people back in: the kid who made the poster, the teacher who tore it down, the hallway full of sixteen-year-olds who mostly wanted lunch.

By Thursday I had two briefs and one headache. Ms. Oliveira caught me in the hallway rehearsing objections to myself, quietly, like a person who should be referred somewhere.

"Which side do you actually believe?" she asked.

"I don't know yet," I said. "Ask me in character."

"That," she said, "is the assignment."

On Friday the courtroom was the lecture hall, with the coach presiding because he owned a gavel, nobody knew why, and forty students who wanted to watch me argue with myself. I stood at the podium for the school first, and I did not use the fire line. I felt it in my pocket like a coin I'd decided not to spend, and I could see Dave in the second row practically vibrating, waiting for it.

"Every generation rediscovers Justice Holmes's theatre," I said instead, "and every generation forgets that in Schenck, in 1919, he wrote it to uphold a conviction. Free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic. That is a true sentence. It is also a sentence with a history, and I am not going to pretend the history is flattering to my side."

Anton mouthed "flattering" at me with his eyebrows up. The coach banged his gavel for no reason. Dave raised his hand even though the audience wasn't supposed to talk, and when the coach ignored him, he raised it higher.

Then it was time to cross the room and become the student's lawyer, and I picked up my notes, and I honestly could not tell you which folder I reached for first.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Any member of the US House of Representatives may introduce a bill in the House, and it is then referred to a committee for study.
story:
The bus idled outside the legislature while Mr. Costa counted heads for the third time, and Blake stood at the back of the line holding the paper he had folded and unfolded so many times that the creases had gone soft. On the paper was a bill. His bill, though he had no right to call it that yet: three paragraphs about funding for school nurses trained to spot early allergic reactions, written at two in the morning after his little brother spent four hours in an emergency room because no one at his school had recognized what was happening until his throat began to swell. Mr. Costa had said the tour would include the gallery and maybe a committee hearing, if the schedules held. Blake had not told anyone why he cared so much about seeing them.

Inside, the marble made everything sound official. Xander leaned toward a portrait of some long-dead speaker and said, "He looks like he's about to tell us we failed something," and Malaya laughed, but quietly, the way people laugh in buildings where laughter seems to require a permit. A guide walked them past the chamber doors, and Blake hung back at the railing above the floor, watching rows of empty desks that would fill later. At the front of the room sat a wooden desk with a small raised platform, and when a page crossed the floor carrying a stack of documents, Blake's attention snagged on the stack the way it snagged on everything now, scanning for the machinery underneath.

The committee hearing was real, which surprised him. He had expected theater, and instead got a long table, a stenographer, and a woman testifying about water rights in a voice so steady it made the room feel lugubrious by contrast, as though gravity itself had been asked to speak. A legislator asked her questions, some sharp, some almost kind. A member of the public had brought an idea here, Blake understood, and the idea was being studied, taken apart, weighed. He copied the words "referred to committee" into the margin of his paper without knowing yet what he would do with them.

During the debate in the gallery that afternoon, he watched a bill about road subsidies get praised, gutted by an amendment, praised again, and then voted down, all within an hour. Malaya, watching the tally board light up green and red, said, "So all that talking, and it just dies?" A man in front of them, a staffer perhaps, turned around and said, not unkindly, "Most of them die. That's not the sad part. The sad part is the ones that die without ever getting heard." Blake's heart began to palpitate, a quick uneven drumming he tried to hide by pressing his palm flat against his thigh.

Afterward, when Mr. Costa released them to the rotunda for twenty minutes, Blake found Xander by the information desk. "You know how a bill even starts?" Xander asked, because Xander asked things like that, rifling the tourist pamphlets. "I asked the desk guy. Any member of the House can introduce one. You write it up, you take it to your representative, and they put it in." He held up a pamphlet as evidence. "Then it gets referred to a committee for study. Like the hearing we saw." Blake took the pamphlet and read the line twice. "So anyone," he said slowly, "can walk an idea in. Through a member." Xander shrugged. "I guess that's the point of them."

Blake sat on the rotunda steps and unfolded his paper one more time. The course was clear now: draft the bill properly, find their representative's email, ask him to introduce it, watch for the committee referral, and then, if it survived, debate, votes, and finally assent before it became law. He understood also, with a coldness that had nothing to do with the marble, that his three paragraphs about nurses and immunology and allergic response would most likely die in a committee room like the one upstairs, unheard, studied to death or simply left on a stack. The path existed, and the path was mostly a graveyard.

Malaya came and sat beside him. "Mr. Costa says five minutes." She looked at the paper in his hands. "Is that your brother thing?" He nodded. "I'm going to email our rep. Ask him to introduce it as a bill." She was quiet for a moment. "Will he?" "I don't know," Blake said. "Any member can do it. Whether one will, that's the part nobody owes you."

On the bus home he drafted the email against the window, deleting and retyping, and by the time the legislature had shrunk to a white dot in the fields behind them, he hit send. The message left his phone with a small whoosh, gone somewhere he could not follow, and outside the window a hawk turned once over the highway and dropped below the treeline.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
Christopher had come to his grandmother's house for the summer with a duffel bag, a bus ticket home in September, and a promise to himself that he would finally learn the piano. The instrument stood against the parlor wall like a polite hostage, walnut-dark, its lid holding a photograph of a man Christopher had never met. He had wanted this for three years without ever saying so, which was, he admitted, a strange way to want something.

He began the way he began everything, with measurement. On the first morning, while the coffee was still too hot and his grandmother was still moving through her diurnal rounds of kettle, crossword, and complaint about the newspaper's font size, he lifted the lid and counted the keys. It was supposed to be simple. A standard piano had 88 keys; he'd learned that from a video at two in the morning, the kind of fact that arrives when you should be asleep and lodges itself permanently. Fifty-two white, thirty-six black. He counted once, lost his place at the black keys, and counted again.

"You're talking to it now," his grandmother said from the kitchen doorway. "That's either dedication or a problem."

"Eighty-five," he said. "I keep getting eighty-five."

"Then count slower." She went back to her crossword, because she was a woman who believed most problems were speed problems.

The number bothered him all afternoon, the way a pebble in a shoe bothers the whole walk. He walked two blocks to the hardware store, where Mr. Russo, who had retired from teaching music in the public schools and now sold people paint brushes with visible sorrow, was restocking. Mr. Russo was also the neighbor who had agreed, for twelve dollars a lesson and the promise of company, to teach Christopher over the summer. The first lesson wasn't until Tuesday, but the counting couldn't wait.

"Eighty-five," Christopher said, before hello.

Mr. Russo set down a brush. "A standard piano has 88 keys," he said. "Fifty-two white and thirty-six black. That's the standard. Now, is your grandmother's piano standard?"

It had not occurred to Christopher that a piano could fail to be standard, that objects could drift from their own definitions just by getting old. He felt slightly betrayed, then slightly delighted. "How old is it?"

"Older than me, probably. Some of those uprights were built before everyone agreed on the number. The low end just stops where it stops." Mr. Russo picked the brush back up. "Count them Tuesday. Bring your eighty-five like a souvenir."

When Jayda and Maryam came through on their drive to a lake neither of them could name on a map, they found Christopher at the piano with masking tape and a marker, labeling the white keys in a system of his own invention.
