He had decided that the missing three keys were not a defect but a fact of the house, the way the third stair creaked and the kitchen tap ran lukewarm forever.

"Very industrial," Jayda said, tapping a taped C. "Is this art or vandalism?"

"It's pedagogy." He played the five-note pattern Mr. Russo had shown him in one free trial session at school, back in spring, badly, twice.

Maryam sat on the bench's edge and watched his hands. "You know the top keys just repeat the bottom ones," she said. "It's all the same twelve, over and over. So honestly, what's missing doesn't even matter. It's relative."

"That is not what relativism means," Christopher said, "and also I refuse to be consoled by philosophy from someone who got lost driving to a lake."

"I didn't get lost. The lake moved."

By August his fingers had begun to habituate themselves to the shapes, so that a C major chord arrived in his hand without being summoned, like a word he'd known all along and only now learned to say. He learned one song completely, a short sad waltz, and played it for his grandmother on a Sunday, and she put down her pen and listened with her head tipped, and afterward said, "Your grandfather played that," which explained the photograph on the lid and made Christopher have to look out the window for a while at nothing in particular.

On his last night, Mr. Russo came by with a folder of sheet music he said Christopher could keep, and stood in the doorway while Christopher played the waltz again. "You'll have a standard piano at college," Mr. Russo said. "Eighty-eight keys. All twelve notes, all the way down." Christopher nodded and kept playing, but his hands kept finding the old octave, the one that ended three notes early, the ending this piano had decided on its own. He played the final chord and let the keys stay down, listening to it fade.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Both countries gain from trade only if the exchange rate between the two goods falls between the two countries' own opportunity costs of making them.
story:
Faith had until Thursday to understand comparative advantage, and by Tuesday evening she still could not make the numbers behave. Ms. Buchanan had announced the quiz with her usual flat cheerfulness, then refused to explain anything further, saying only that the farmers' market on Caldwell Road was open until six. "Look at what people actually do," she had said, stacking papers, already half out the door. So on Wednesday Faith went, notebook sequestered in her backpack like contraband, because if she was going to fail, she would at least fail having tried something.

The market occupied a cracked parking lot behind the church. One stall sold apples in woven baskets; the other, two spaces down, sold honey in squat jars. Faith bought a small apple with her last two dollars and stood near the honey stall pretending to examine a jar of beeswax candles while she listened. The apple woman, broad-shouldered and sunburnt, was arguing with the honey man in the low, affectionate growl of people who have quarreled for years.

"A basket of my apples is worth three jars of your honey," the apple woman said. "At least three. It takes me all season."

"You're dreaming. One jar. One jar of honey for a whole basket."

Faith wrote both numbers down. Three jars, one jar. In her textbook the two countries were called Alphaland and Betaland, which had always struck her as a particularly lazy form of fiction, and she had spent an hour Monday night trying to memorize which one made what and at what cost, and the whole structure had collapsed when she turned the page. But here were the two stallholders, alive and irritated, and their argument had a shape. Three jars was what the apple woman gave up, in honey she could have made herself, to fill a basket. One jar was the same sacrifice for the honey man. Or something like that. She was not sure yet, and she did not pretend to be.

She found a bench by the church wall and worked. If a basket of apples traded for three jars, exactly, then the apple woman gained nothing; she might as well make her own honey. If it traded for one jar, the honey man gained nothing. So anything between one and three jars, she thought, both of them came out ahead. Anything outside that range, one of them was simply losing. She checked it twice with the numbers written in the margin of her quiz review sheet, then a third time, because the maxim of Ms. Buchanan's class, printed above every worksheet, was that trade is positive sum, and Faith had never once been asked to say when it wasn't.

Malaika arrived at five, having promised to study with her, and flopped onto the bench with a bottle of iced tea. "Ms. Buchanan told me you'd be here. Did you figure out the thing?"

"I think so. The price has to fall between what it costs each of them." Faith turned the notebook so Malaika could see. "Between one and three jars for a basket. That's the whole idea, I think. The book calls it comparative advantage."

"Then go tell them their marriage is saved."

Faith laughed, then didn't, because she realized she was nervous. Walking up to two strangers in a parking lot to explain their own haggling to them felt, at first, like an atavistic terror, some old animal caution about approaching a fire where you were not invited. But the market was closing in twenty minutes, and Thursday was less than a day away, and she wanted to know if the idea held up outside her notebook.

The two stallholders were still at it, though wearily now, packing crates in each other's company. "Excuse me," Faith said. "I couldn't help hearing. If a basket of apples is worth three jars to you, and one jar to you, then any deal between those two numbers makes you both better off. Two jars. Two and a half. Anywhere in that range."

The honey man scratched his jaw. The apple woman looked at Faith, then at the last basket of apples going soft in the heat, then at the honey man. "Two jars," she said.

"Two jars and a pint of the little ones," he said, and they shook on it, and Faith walked back to the bench with the feeling of having held something up in the air and found that it held her too, or part of her weight anyway, the part that trusted that problems had insides you could learn.

She and Malaika stayed until the stalls were folded down, and it was nearly dark when the honey man loaded his truck and stopped beside their bench. "You know," he said, jerking his chin toward the apple woman's taillights, "she's my sister. Twenty years we've been swapping apples and honey, every Wednesday. Two jars." He climbed in and pulled the door shut. "You did the arithmetic, though. Nice to finally meet the referee."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
Landon arrived at the camp gate twenty minutes early, which for him was a kind of miracle, and stood in the smell of cut grass and chlorine drifting up from the pool. Beyond the fence, little kids in orange lanyards were already shrieking around the tetherball pole. Ms. Desir, the program director, met the new junior counselors under the pavilion with a clipboard and a stack of manila folders, and handed each of them a form Landon had never seen before. At the top it said Form I-9, Employment Eligibility Verification.

"Section 1 is yours," Ms. Desir said. "It's due no later than your first day of paid work, and this is your first day of paid work, so today counts."

Landon's father had an adage he liked to inculcate at every opportunity, usually over dishes: the prepared man is never surprised. Landon had heard it so often it had become impervious to him, sliding off like water off the pool slide. He had assumed, all summer, that paperwork came after the first paycheck, once the job had proven itself real. Justine, who sat beside him with her folder already dog-eared, had apparently assumed otherwise.

"I did mine last night," Justine said, sliding her completed form out like a receipt she'd been saving. "My mom printed it from the website."

"Of course you did," Landon said, but without heat, because Justine had also laminated her camp nametag, and there was something almost admirable in that level of readiness. Madeleine, on his other side, was reading her form with her chin propped on her fist, squinting at the citizenship checkboxes like they were written in a foreign language.

Landon looked down at his own copy. It wanted his address, his date of birth, a choice of boxes about citizenship, and an attestation he was supposed to sign. It did not, he realized with a slow tightening in his stomach, want the passport that was sitting in a drawer at home, or the social security card he had used exactly once, to open a bank account. He turned the page over, then back, as if the form might have printed differently the second time.

"I don't have my documents," he said to Ms. Desir, keeping his voice low so the kids at the tetherball pole wouldn't hear a junior counselor admitting to being unprepared on day one.

She tapped the top section of the page. "You completed Section 1 today, which is what's required of you by today. You're fine. And before you ask, no, you can't finish it tonight, because tonight wouldn't be your first day of paid work. Today is."

He filled in his address, checked the first box, and signed, and the signature looked strangely adult, slanted and quick, not the careful letters he used on birthday cards. Around him the pavilion filled with the scratch of pens. Madeleine asked Justine what "attestation" meant, and Justine said it meant you were swearing the thing was true, and Madeleine said that sounded like a lot of pressure for a summer job handing out juice boxes.

Afterward they walked the perimeter of the pool together, learning where the first aid kit hung and which gate had to stay latched, and Landon found himself revising something he'd carried around without examining it. His father's adage, it turned out, wasn't wrong, exactly; it just wasn't the whole truth. Being prepared had mattered this morning, but so had knowing what preparation actually meant in this case, one section of one form, on one day, and not the whole ceremony of a passport and a solemn oath. He could hold both ideas now, the prepared man and the man who reads the instructions, without deciding which one was really his. Some of it, like what Ms. Desir did with the forms after she collected them, he simply didn't know yet.

By lunch, the sun had flattened the shade under the pavilion to a thin blue line, and the three of them sat eating sandwiches while the campers napped on mats. Justine was telling a story about a camper who had hidden a frog in the craft bin, and Landon was half listening, mostly watching the gate, where a station wagon had pulled up and a woman was unloading a carseat and a diaper bag and a folder of her own. She called something to Ms. Desir across the grass, apologetic, and Landon caught the words late, sorry, and today, right?

Ms. Desir raised her clipboard toward the wagon and said, "If she's here to get paid, she fills out Section 1 before she goes home."

Madeleine leaned over and whispered, "That's the new swim teacher, isn't it?"

"It's somebody's first day," Landon said, and took the last bite of his sandwich.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Sikh gurdwara's langar serves free vegetarian meals to anyone regardless of religion, caste or status, and people traditionally eat together seated on the floor as equals.
story:
Noah had told Hussain almost nothing, which felt, on the bus ride over, like a small subterfuge. "It's a thing at my family's gurdwara," he'd said. "Vaisakhi. There's food. Just wear something you can sit on the floor in." Hussain, who was laconic by nature and had spent three years of high school saying less than necessary, had answered only, "Cool," and put his earbuds back in. Now they were walking up the driveway, and Noah was wondering why he hadn't just explained. Maybe because explaining would have meant deciding what it meant to him first.

His mother was already inside, tying a fresh scarf over her hair in the lobby. She greeted Hussain with the particular warmth she reserved for Noah's friends, which was warmer than the warmth she reserved for Noah. In the hall, they covered their heads and took off their shoes, and Hussain did it all without being asked twice, though Noah caught him glancing at the carpet where hundreds of shoes sat in patient rows, and at the elderly man carefully laying a rug runner along the floor.

They sat through the service because Noah's grandfather wanted them to, and Noah found himself doing the arithmetic he always did at these things. At school he was Noah who played centre back and didn't talk about religion. Here he was Simranjeet's grandson, the one studying in the city. He had gotten good at keeping the two rooms separate, and he understood that this was a kind of compartmentalizing, and he understood, less comfortablyably, that he had never decided whether it was tidiness or cowardice. Hussain sat beside him with his palms open on his knees, watching the musicians the way he watched a match he didn't yet understand the rules of, quietly working out the pattern.

Afterward came the part Noah had actually wanted Hussain to see. Downstairs, the langar hall was filling, and they joined a line of volunteers rolling out thin rotis at a hot stove, some of them teenagers, one of them a woman Noah recognized as his dentist. "You can help," Noah said, and they did, for twenty minutes, filling steel trays and carrying them to the rows of people already seated cross-legged on the floor.

"Wait," Hussain said, pausing with a tray in his hands. "Everyone sits on the floor?" He looked down the long rows, at the professor from the university and the man who came in ragged from the street eating side by side, at Noah's grandfather and at a table of students. "Everyone."

"On the floor," Noah said. "As equals." He said it and heard how it sounded, like a slogan, and wished he had let Hussain just see it instead. But Hussain was nodding slowly, still scanning the room.

"Free too?"

"Free. Vegetarian. Anyone. Doesn't matter your religion, doesn't matter your caste, doesn't matter anything." Noah set his tray down on the stack. "That's the whole point of it."

They sat eventually, cross-legged, plates of dal and rice before them on the floor, and a volunteer came by with a bucket and a ladle, refilling cups of water. Hussain ate for a while in silence, which Noah had learned was his way of thinking. Noah's grandfather, two rows ahead, turned around at one point and asked Hussain where his family was from, and listened to the answer with real attention, and told him his daughter had lived in Karachi for a year, and Hussain's face opened in a way Noah had never seen in a cafeteria.

"So you never told me any of this," Hussain said, when the grandfather had turned back. It wasn't an accusation. It was more like curiosity, the same tone he used about the offside rule.
Noah pushed the rice around his plate. "I don't know why. I guess I thought you'd find it, I don't know. Strange."
"It is strange," Hussain said. "In the good way. Like, at the mosque we have iftar, everyone eats, but this is, there's no tables at all. The floor thing. That's the part." He gestured with his roti at the whole hall, the rows extending toward the kitchen. "Nobody's higher than anybody. It's not a symbol, it's just, literally the floor."

Noah looked at the room as if for the first time, at his dentist ladling dal, at his grandfather sitting on the same carpet as a stranger in torn shoes, and thought about the two rooms he kept in his head, school and here, and how Hussain had walked into one of them without knocking and the walls had not come down but had begun, at least, to seem thinner. Whether he would tear them down himself, whether he would start saying the whole of it out loud at school, he genuinely did not know, and it surprised him a little that not knowing felt less like failure than like standing in a doorway.

In the lobby, putting their shoes back on, Hussain paused with one shoe in his hand. "Next time there's a thing at the mosque," he said, "you're coming."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: If two countries give up exactly the same amount of one good to make the other, neither has a comparative advantage, and Ricardo's model predicts no gain from specializing.
story:
Mr. Farah-Ali had left the answer key on the desk at the front of the room while he graded essays in the corner, and Elijah sat three rows back with the textbook problem in front of him and a growing suspicion that the answer key was wrong. The problem gave two countries, Aland and Belmar, each making coffee and steel. Aland gave up two tons of coffee for every ton of steel it produced. Belmar, the numbers said, gave up two tons of coffee for every ton of steel too. The question asked who should specialize in what, and the key said, in the terse way of keys everywhere, that trade would not help either country.

"There has to be a mistake," Elijah said. He turned his notebook toward Keanna, who was highlighting her own textbook in four colors, which struck him as a genuinely excessive number of colors. "Look. If Aland makes steel, it gives up two tons of coffee. If Belmar makes steel, it also gives up two tons of coffee. Same trade-off, both sides."

Keanna set down the green highlighter. "So who's better at steel?"

"Neither. That's the thing. They're identical." He tapped the page. "But the whole chapter is about how trade helps everybody. There's a graph. The graph has arrows. It's very confident."

Shane, who had been drawing a sullen turtle in the margin of his notes, looked up. "Maybe the turtle knows," he said. "Maybe the turtle is an economist." His stoicism about the upcoming exam had been remarked on by several people; he claimed not to care, though he had also claimed this while making forty flashcards.

Elijah worked the ratios again in the margin, slowly, because he distrusted his own arithmetic more than he distrusted the textbook. Coffee per steel: two for Aland. Coffee per steel: two for Belmar. He flipped it, steel per coffee: one half for both. He sat back. "They give up exactly the same amount of one good to make the other," he said. "Both of them. So the book is saying that when that happens, neither one has a comparative advantage."

Keanna wrote the term down. "That's the phrase from Tuesday."

"Right, but Tuesday the ratios were different. Portugal and England or whatever. One of them was worse at both things and trade still worked, that was the whole point, that it doesn't matter if you're worse at everything." He paused. "And now the one case where it stops working walks in the door."

He got up and crossed to the front, where Mr. Farah-Ali sat with a stack of essays on the French Revolution, one of which he was apparently reading with the expression of a man being slowly eulogized by a student who had confused Robespierre with Napoleon. Elijah waited until he looked up.

"The problem on page 214," Elijah said. "Aland and Belmar. The key says trade doesn't help. Is that a typo?"

Mr. Farah-Ali set down his pen. "What did you get?"

"Two tons of coffee per ton of steel, for both of them. Exactly the same. So I thought, no comparative advantage, so no reason for either of them to specialize. But I wanted to check, because every other problem in the chapter has trade helping."

"Every other problem in the chapter has different ratios," Mr. Farah-Ali said. "You checked the arithmetic?"

"Twice. Shane checked a third time, sort of, in between the turtle."

From three rows back, Shane held up the turtle without comment.

"Then the key is right," Mr. Farah-Ali said, and returned to his essay, and Elijah stood there a moment longer, because he had wanted a different answer and had known, even while wanting it, that wanting had nothing to do with it. He walked back to his seat.

"So the model just says no," Keanna said.

"The model says no when it's exactly like this. Same give-up on both sides, and there's nothing to gain from specializing." He looked at the arrows on the graph in the chapter, the confident arrows, and then at his own margin where the two identical ratios sat side by side. "What I can't tell is whether that ever actually happens. Real countries, real numbers. Whether it's a real edge case or just something they put in a problem set."

Keanna uncapped the green highlighter again. "So write that."

"What, that I don't know?"

"That you don't know, on the page, where he's going to read it." She slid her notebook over to show her own margins, which were full of small bracketed questions she had apparently been asking textbooks all year without telling anyone.

Elijah read her smallest question, which was whether the Revolutionary calendar counted leap years, and decided that his margins had been underused his whole life. He wrote, beneath the two ratios, "not sure this occurs outside problem sets, will look for a real example," and then, after a moment, drew a small turtle beside it for Shane's benefit.

Shane leaned over, studied it, and said, "That turtle has a comparative advantage in nothing."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
Ryder taped the cones into two lines along the gym floor before the eighth graders arrived, spacing them the width of a lacrosse pass, and stepped back to see whether the lanes he had built looked anything like the ones that collapsed on Saturday. They lost 9-4, and all nine goals came off turnovers in the middle third, the ball thrown blind into a swarm of sticks. He had watched it happen from the bench and felt something he could not name at first, a kind of itch, because the team had practised all season and practised the same thing every time. Scrimmage, scrimmage, scrimmage. Forty minutes of playing, and the passing never got cleaner.

The itch followed him into Monday. In Mr. Lavoie's class they were arguing about how historians choose what counts as evidence, and Mr. Lavoie wrote "historiography" on the board, the study not of the past itself but of how the past gets written. Ryder copied the word down and then stopped writing, because it struck him that his team had a history too, one he had been authoring: every practice that ended in scrimmage was another page saying this is what improvement looks like. When Matteo, two seats over, tried to problematize the textbook's claim that sources should be primary, asking whether a diary lies as easily as a newspaper does, Ryder was only half listening. He was thinking about the gym.

He found the study that night, chasing a half-remembered phrase from a video he'd watched instead of doing homework. In 1993, K. Anders Ericsson and some colleagues had studied violinists, and the finding was strange and simple at once. What separated the best players was not hours logged but something they called deliberate practice: effortful work aimed at a specific weakness, with immediate feedback. Effortful, specific, feedback. Ryder read the sentence three times, and each time the gym in his head rearranged itself a little. Scrimmage gave the team hours and fun and almost no feedback at all. Nobody stopped a bad pass to say why it was bad.

The eighth graders filed in on Tuesday already groaning, because Emerik, the smallest and loudest of them, had announced at lunch that Ryder was cancelling scrimmage forever. "That's not what I said," Ryder told them, gathering them around the whiteboard. He had written one word on it. "Deliberate practice," he said. "That's what it's called." Emerik folded his arms and said that deliberate practice sounded like homework, and that homework was already ruining his life. This was Emerik's whole project, as far as Ryder could tell, to defend lacrosse as the one place left with no obligations attached, and Ryder realized he was about to take even that from him, a little.

The drill was ugly by design. Five passes, then a shot, and every pass had to hit a shooter moving through the lane between the cones; if the ball arrived late, they ran it again, and Ryder called out the reason in the moment, early, early, you waited on him. The first twenty minutes were chaos. Kids stared at their sticks as if the sticks had betrayed them. But in the third rotation Emerik caught a pass on the run, in stride, without breaking rhythm, and even he went quiet for a second, surprised by his own hands. "Again," he said, before Ryder could say it. "Run that again."

By Thursday the middle third was different. Not fixed, exactly. Ryder kept a notebook now, and in it he tracked what the drills still missed, how a kid could nail the lane in practice and still freeze when a defender's stick came at his ribs, and he honestly did not know whether that gap closed with more cones or with the real pressure of games. Maybe some weaknesses only showed up under conditions you could not build. He had started wondering, too, whether the violinists' teachers had faced the same wall, though that was a stretch he had no way to test from a gym in a school with a row of arboreal giants swaying outside the high windows, dropping acorns on the roof of the equipment shed.

On Saturday they lost 7-6, and the six goals they scored all began with passes that led the cutter, that found the open lane where a month ago there had been only a crowd. After the game Emerik hung back while the others shuffled toward the change room, and stood turning his stick over in his hands. "So next week," he said, "are we doing the cones, or are we scrimmaging?"

Ryder looked down the empty floor, at the scuff marks where the lane had been, and heard the acorns ticking off the shed roof. "Both," he said, and picked up the ball bag.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Accounting profit subtracts only money actually paid out, while economic profit also subtracts implicit costs such as the owner's time and the next-best use of their money.
story:
Mackenzie had the scholarship essay open on her laptop and forty minutes until the midnight deadline when Alexis called. The bedroom window was cracked and the sound of the sprinklers came through it, ticking across the neighbours' lawn like a clock with a grudge. "I need you to look at something," Alexis said, and Mackenzie could hear her fan whirring in the background, the same cheap fan she'd had since seventh grade.

"Can it be tomorrow?"

"It's about the shop. Someone wants to buy it. I have to answer by morning."

The shop sold enamel pins Alexis designed, mostly mushrooms and small moons, and Mackenzie had watched her build it from the bedroom floor two summers ago, cutting bubble mailers with craft scissors while the desktop fan burnished everything with its steady noise. Alexis had said then, and said often since, that she was making money. Real money. Enough that she talked about skipping the college tour her mother had planned.

Mackenzie minimized the essay, which was 214 words of a required 500, and pulled up a spreadsheet. "Okay. Tell me what you actually paid out this year. Pins, shipping, the website."

Alexis read numbers from her phone: two hundred and forty on supplies, ninety on the site, a little for packaging. Revenue, after the platform's cut, came to eleven hundred. Mackenzie typed it. "So you cleared, what, seven hundred."

"See? Making money."

"How many hours?"

There was a pause long enough for the sprinklers to turn off. "I don't count hours."

"Estimate."

Alexis estimated. Designing, packing, answering messages, standing in line at the post office: Mackenzie watched the number climb and typed it in. Two hundred and ten hours, roughly, at the eleven dollars an hour Alexis earned at the bakery before the shop ate her Saturdays. The cell Mackenzie computed came out negative, and she turned the screen toward the window as if Alexis could see it through the phone.

"Accounting profit only subtracts what you paid out," Alexis said slowly, and Mackenzie realized she was reading, that there was an economics textbook open somewhere in that other bedroom. "Economic profit also subtracts what you gave up. Your time. What your money could have earned somewhere else." She laughed, but not the way she laughed at jokes. "So I've been losing money for two years and calling it a business."

Mackenzie, who was obdurate about deadlines in a way her friends found tiresome, nevertheless kept typing, building the second column, the honest one, while the clock in the corner of her screen moved from 11:21 to 11:34. She thought about her own essay, the half-formed paragraph about the summer she'd given up soccer for a job at the pool, about how she'd framed that as sacrifice and discipline. She had become a revisionist about it, honestly, editing the memory each time so that the choice looked nobler than the boredom had felt. The truth was she'd wanted the money and told herself a better story. Alexis was doing the opposite: calling a loss a profit out of affection for the thing itself.

"Who's buying it?" Mackenzie asked.

"Aria."

The word sat there. Aria, who had a full ride to the state school and no job and a laptop that already ran design software, whose next-best use of two hundred hours was nothing at all. Mackenzie did the arithmetic without saying it aloud. For Aria, the implicit costs were nearly zero. The same shop, the same pins, the same seven hundred dollars, and a positive economic profit. It wasn't that Alexis had been wrong to build it or that Aria was smarter. The shop hadn't changed. The alternatives had.

"Eleven fifty," Mackenzie said, looking at the clock. Her essay stood at 231 words. There was time to write maybe two hundred more, or time to say the true thing to Alexis, but not both, and she sat with her fingers above the keys, feeling the cost of each one before she'd paid it.

"Sell it," Mackenzie said. "For the pins and the customer list, get eight hundred. Aria will still come out ahead."

"Then I'll be a girl who lost two years."

"Then you'll be a girl with eight hundred dollars and every Saturday."

Alexis was quiet. "What are you not doing right now to tell me this?"

Mackenzie looked at the essay, the cursor blinking in the empty half of the page, and back at the phone. "Nothing important," she said, and opened a new document to type the eight-hundred-dollar offer into an email before she could count what it cost her.

"Send me the essay when it's done," Alexis said. "I'll read it on the bakery shift you're going to quit."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for libel must prove actual malice: that the statement was known to be false or made with reckless disregard for truth.
story:
Charlie had spread both briefs across the library table like opposing armies, the left side arguing that the Clarion should pay for calling the mayor a criminal, the right side arguing it should not, and somewhere in the middle lay a paperback constitutional law text she'd pulled from the stacks an hour ago. She had been the one who volunteered to argue both sides in Monday's mock court, mostly because Mr. Ferreira had said it was the hardest job, and partly because she wanted to know whether she believed either side at all.

"How can you argue against the newspaper when you wrote for the school paper?" Kayla asked, dropping into the chair across from her with a granola bar and no books. Kayla wanted the editor-in-chief job next year and had been campaigning quietly for weeks, which meant she wanted Charlie's endorsement at the meeting on Tuesday, which meant she had suddenly become very available for study sessions.

"That's the problem," Charlie said. "I keep drafting the newspaper side and it turns into a platitude. Truth matters. Press freedom matters. The watchdog of democracy. It sounds like a poster in a guidance counselor's office." She slid a page across the table. "The other side is more interesting and I hate that it is."

Kayla read it, chewing. The other side said the Clarion had printed that the mayor took bribes, the mayor had never taken bribes, and a retraction buried on page nine did not repair a reputation. It said a paper that big, covering a mayor that closely, should have checked before it printed. That felt true to Charlie too, which was the unsettling part.

She went back to the stacks alone, to the shelf where the real cases lived, and found the 1964 case Mr. Ferreira had circled on her assignment sheet. New York Times v. Sullivan. She read the holding twice, then a third time, mouthing it. The Supreme Court had held that a public official suing for libel must prove actual malice: that the statement was known to be false or made with reckless disregard for truth. She sat down on the carpet between the shelves, holding the book open on her knees, and felt the whole argument shift under her. The mayor could not simply show the story was wrong. Wrongness wasn't enough. He had to prove the paper knew, or didn't care whether it knew, and that was a different thing entirely, a thing about the inside of someone's head.

"Actual malice," she said out loud to the empty aisle, testing the phrase. "That's what it's called."

When she came back to the table, Scott was there, which was itself a small event, because Scott had skipped the last two practice rounds. He was arguing the mayor's side on Monday, against her, and he had the grim look of someone who had just discovered the same case she had. "It's rigged," he said before she sat down. "You get to make me prove what a newspaper knew in its heart. How do you even do that?"

"You look for evidence of it," Charlie said. "What did they have before they published, who did they call, did anyone say stop." She was already hearing her own voice slide into the newspaper's side, the side she had thought was the boring side, and she noticed the slide and let it happen.

Scott leaned over her brief. "So wait. You're going to argue the error about the mayor shouldn't be punished unless I can show actual malice. And when I ask you how a public official is supposed to prove reckless disregard, you're going to say that's the price we pay for an uninhibited press." He frowned at the page. "That's a platitude with a footnote."

"It's a platitude I can now support with the holding," Charlie said, but she said it slowly, because something was turning over in her. She had spent a week certain the interesting side was the mayor's, the human side, the side of a wronged man. Now she saw that the case wasn't really about him at all. It was about a rule that deliberately made his burden heavy so that the rest of them could keep arguing in print, even badly, even sometimes wrongly. She tried to hold both truths in her hands at once and found they fit, awkwardly, like two halves of something hinged. "I still think the paper was sloppy," she said. "I'm just not sure sloppy is what the Court wanted to punish."

Kayla, who had been quiet, bent over her phone. "The Clarion's ombudsman column from 2019," she said, turning the screen around. "They got a county auditor's name wrong once and never corrected it until he sued, and he lost because he couldn't prove they knew. It's like your case, but real, and small." She looked up with the particular brightness she wore when being helpful strategically. "This could go in the paper next year. My section, if I get it."

Charlie looked at Kayla, then at the column, then at Scott's notes, where he had already crossed out half his outline. He had come in angry about a rigged fight; now he was rebuilding his case around the gap she'd shown him, planning to make her prove that the Clarion hadn't known, which was, she admitted, the same impossible burden pointed the other way. Somewhere in that reversal was a fairness she hadn't expected from him.

"I don't know how Monday ends," she told them, gathering her pages into one stack, both sides face to face. "I think I believe the newspaper should win and I think the mayor was wronged and I haven't figured out how to say both without sounding like I'm hedging."

"That's the actual malice of your position," Scott said. "Reckless disregard for knowing what you think."

She laughed and slid the library book across to him, open to the marked page, its margins already soft with her pencil.

"Read it yourself," she said. "Then come fight me."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
The line outside the community centre reached the corner before Vincent had even finished tying the apron strings behind his back. He had expected a handful of people, maybe a few families down on their luck, and he had volunteered mostly because Arya had badgered him into it and because the form said the food bank shared its building with the animal shelter, which meant he could walk the dogs afterward. Now he stood at a folding table stacked with canned tomatoes and rice, watching the queue shuffle forward in the grey light of a Tuesday morning, and felt something in his chest go quiet.

"It's always like this," Arya said, snapping on gloves beside him. "Weekdays are worse, actually. People come before shifts, or after night shifts, or on their lunch break from jobs that don't cover rent." She said it without drama, the way she reported everything, which was why people at school half-joked she should run a newspaper.

Mr. Nowak, who ran both the food bank and the shelter, moved along the table behind them, straightening boxes. He had a way of occupying a room without raising his voice, a slow, deliberate gravitas that made even the barking from the kennels next door seem organized. "Vincent, you're on hampers with Misha," he said. "Ask each person if they have an oven. It matters more than you'd think."

Misha turned out to be a wiry boy from Vincent's chemistry class whom Vincent barely knew, though he knew of him, because in September everyone had briefly lionized Misha after he'd caught a mistake in the textbook that the teacher had confirmed was real. Misha had spent the following week looking faintly embarrassed, and he looked that way now too, hauling a crate of pasta like a boy trying not to be noticed for being strong.

The first hour taught Vincent more than the orientation video had. He learned to ask about ovens, and about allergies, and about whether there were babies, because formula was kept in a locked cabinet at the back. He learned that a man in a delivery uniform could be polite and exhausted and out the door in four minutes flat. He learned that an elderly woman would linger over the choice between tea and coffee as though the decision carried weight, and that it did, and that rushing her would have been a kind of theft.

It was somewhere in that hour that he got it wrong. A young mother with a stroller remarked, almost apologetically, that the line seemed longer every month, and Vincent, wanting to seem informed, said, "Yeah, I read it was pretty bad, like a million visits or something." Arya looked up from her clipboard. "It's higher," she said. "HungerCount 2025. Nearly 2.2 million food bank visits across Canada in one month, March 2025. A record for a single month." She said it the way she said everything, flat and exact, and then she handed the woman a bag of apples and said, "These are the good ones, they came in this morning," and the moment passed, except that it didn't pass for Vincent at all.

He kept filling hampers while the number sat in him, refusing to become background. Two point two million in a single month. He had spent the summer arguing with his father about politics at the dinner table, holding one position the way you hold a shield, and he had started college applications essays about service without ever having served anything. And meanwhile there was this: a Tuesday line to the corner, a locked cabinet of formula, Arya's flat voice reciting a fact the way you'd read a weather report before a storm. He wasn't sure what he thought should be done about it, and he was suspicious of anyone who was sure, having been that person himself at dinner two weeks ago. But he noticed he had stopped composing arguments in his head and started counting cans instead, and that this felt like information too.

Near closing, a boy about ten years old, waiting with his grandmother, pressed his face to the interior door that connected to the shelter. Through it, a muffled chorus of barking rose and fell. "You can go look," Mr. Nowak told him. "The dogs don't mind visitors." The boy hesitated, glanced at his grandmother, who nodded, and slipped through the door. A minute later they heard him laugh, a sudden bright sound through the wall, and the grandmother closed her eyes for a second, still holding her hamper.

When the last person had gone, Misha began restacking shelves without being asked, and Arya started on the dishes nobody had assigned her. "That kid," Misha said, nodding toward the door. "Some people would say a dog is a gratuitous expense when you can barely feed people." He set down a can. "Those people have never watched a kid laugh like that." Vincent pulled his gloves off, one finger at a time. "I'm coming back Thursday," he said. "And after, I'm walking a dog. Want to come?" Misha looked at him for a moment, then reached for the next crate.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
The playground at dusk was where the cheer squad practised when the gym got double-booked, and tonight the gym had gotten double-booked, which meant their mats were laid out between the swing set and the rusted climbing dome while Coach checked her phone every few minutes. Regionals was Saturday. That gave them one full practice, one afternoon, to fix what everyone privately agreed was broken and no one would say aloud: Elaine's tumbling section came in late, every time, and because Elaine anchored the pyramid, her lateness pulled the whole routine out of sync.

Savannah had been chewing on the problem since Tuesday, when Elaine had rushed her pass, landed short, and Gracelyn, catching her, had said "you ruined the transition" in front of the freshmen. Elaine had gone quiet for the rest of practice in a way that Savannah recognized, because it was the same quiet she herself wore when she was deciding whether to come back at all. Nobody had apologized. Nobody had said anything since.

She had gone looking, Wednesday night, through an old psychology paperback her mother had left on the porch, and found a chapter about a psychologist named Thomas Gordon who had promoted something called I-messages back in the 1960s. The idea was that you said "I felt stuck when the slides came in late" instead of "you ruined it," and the sentence changed shape because the blame drained out of it. Savannah had read the page twice, then copied one of the patterns into her notes app, below a grocery list and a reminder about her deposit for the dorm. It felt almost too simple to work.

Gracelyn, stretching by the chain-link fence, saw Savannah watching Elaine and read her mind with the blunt accuracy of someone who had been her best friend since fourth grade. "If you're going to say something to her, say it fast," Gracelyn said. "We don't have another practice after this."

"I know." Savannah twisted her wrists, untwisted them. "That's the problem. I get one shot and I'll say it wrong."

Gracelyn shrugged, which was Gracelyn's way of saying she agreed it was possible. She did not offer to do it herself. That, at least, was honest; Gracelyn's honesty ran virulent when she was frustrated, an infection that spread through a practice fast, and she seemed to know it. The counterpoint was Savannah, who could go whole seasons saying nothing at all, and both of them had watched that combination nearly break the team last year when the uniforms got ordered two sizes wrong and nobody with the invoice had wanted to be the one to bring it up.

Savannah spent the water break drafting sentences in her head. She tried "you're always late on the tumbling pass" and felt the sentence collapse into accusation before it even reached her mouth. She tried "the routine's a mess" and that was worse, a vague thing that would aggrandize the problem until it filled the whole playground while telling Elaine nothing she could actually use. The book's version was narrower and, she realized, more demanding: it made her name what she had felt, and when, and it forced her to be specific. She waited until Elaine came off the mat towelling her neck, and walked her over to the swings, out of the circle of the coach's voice.

"I need to tell you something before Saturday," Savannah said, and felt her pulse tick up. "It's not a blame thing. It's an I-message, that's the term, I got it from this book. I felt like the whole pyramid was about to collapse when you started the pass late tonight, because I'm locked underneath you and I can't see you coming." She heard how strange the words were, borrowed, and kept going anyway. "If you started the pass on Gracelyn's count instead of waiting to hear the music, I think it fixes it."

Elaine held the towel in both hands and looked at the rubber ground under the swings for a long moment. "I wait for the music because I lost the count at the qualifier," she said. "I got scared I'd come in early instead." It was the first she had said about the qualifier to anyone. They worked it out on the spot, a compromise Savannah hadn't planned: Graclyn would call the count louder, which was a small job for someone whose voice already carried across a parking lot, and Elaine would trust it. Coach let them run the pyramid three more times before the lights in the park switched on and everything went amber.

On the third run, Elaine's pass came in exactly on the count, and the pyramid held, all of them stacked and steady for two full beats before the dismount. Gracelyn's hands found Elaine's shoulders on the landing, and Coach shouted something about Saturday that the wind took half of. Savannah didn't know yet whether it would hold under the lights and the noise of an actual arena, and she was honest enough with herself to admit that she didn't; one good practice was one good practice. She only knew that Elaine was still here, and laughing, and that on Monday, when the uniforms came in, she knew exactly how she was going to tell the coach about the sleeves.

"Again," Coach called, tapping her phone. "From the top."

Savannah jogged back to her spot and set her feet.

The mower had eaten its last bolt sometime in June, and Anthony's grandfather had responded by leaving it in the middle of the garden like a monument, so Anthony spent the first week of his stay at the grandparents' house operationalizing a simpler plan: pull weeds, carry water, and rehearse. He was to be a peer health educator at his college orientation in September, the one first-year who had volunteered, and he had a script to learn. Consent, contraception, testing. He practiced on his grandmother while she shelled peas, and she was a merciless audience.

"So you're saying if my Harold wanted to dance with me and I said no, he'd have to just live with that," she said, flicking a pea into the bowl.

"Even if you danced with him yesterday. Even if you're married. Yes."

"Good. I'll tell him at dinner." She tipped the bowl toward him. "You explain things without wiggling around. Your father wiggles."

It was Nikolai's message, arriving that evening while Anthony sat on the porch with the script highlighters spread around him, that turned rehearsal into performance. Need help. It's Nixon. Pharmacy thing. Can I call. Then, before Anthony could answer: He's here. Putting him on.

Nixon's voice came through the phone thin and too fast. He and a girl from his summer league had, in his words, gotten careless, and now it was nearly nine at night, and he wanted to know if there was anything to be done or if the whole matter was simply sealed and mailed. He had a querulous edge he couldn't hide, the voice of a boy asking for a refund on a decision. Anthony's grandfather, who was listening from his chair with his hearing aid turned generously up, said, "Nixon can drive. The pharmacy on Marsh Street is open till ten. Take my car, and bring back change from the disbursement, I want the receipt." He held out the keys as if this were a routine errand, like collecting a newspaper.

Anthony drove. Nixon sat in the passenger seat with his hood up, which was its own kind of joke, since there was no one to hide from at nine at night, and Anthony let him have it. Nikolai came along because, as he put it, "I'm the one who read the pamphlet, I'm management." At the pharmacy the pharmacist was a small woman in a green vest who took one look at the three of them and said, "Emergency contraception?" with the tone of someone guessing the weather.

"Is it too late?" Nixon asked. "It's been, like, twelve hours."

"Twelve hours is fine. It works mainly by delaying ovulation, and it's more effective the sooner you take it after unprotected sex." She set the box on the counter. "So tonight is better than tomorrow, and tomorrow is much better than waiting a few days."

"Because it delays the egg coming out," Nikolai said, mostly to prove he'd read the pamphlet.

"I said what I said," the pharmacist said, ringing it up. "The box has the rest. Are you paying, or is your friend?"

Nixon paid with a card he had to hunt for through three pockets, and outside in the parking lot he stood holding the paper bag as though it were something that might go off. Anthony, feeling the script in his back pocket like a cheat sheet, asked him, "Do you know about testing? Because that pamphlet can't tell you everything. There's a clinic near campus, it's free, you just book online."

"I don't have anything," Nixon said, then, quieter, "I don't know that."

"That's the whole point of testing. You don't have to guess. You go, they take a sample or they give you a kit, you get results in a week or so, and then you know instead of worrying in a hood."

"I wasn't hiding," Nixon said, taking the hood down anyway. "It was cold."

"Course it was," Nikolai said. "Freezing in July."

At the grandparents' house, the grandfather inspected the receipt, pronounced the change correct to the dollar, and asked no questions at all, which Anthony understood to be its own form of grace. The next morning Nixon texted a photo of the clinic's booking page with a Thursday slot highlighted, and one line underneath: booked it, don't tell my brother, also your grandma says hi, she beat me at cards at the gas station, how is that possible. Anthony wrote back that it was possible because she had been playing since before Nixon's father was born, and that Thursday was a good day for it. Then he took the mower's bolt down to the hardware store to match it, the script still in his back pocket, going soft at the corners from being carried everywhere, like a thing that had finally been used.
